The resulting estimator, gradient descent on the fit loss followed by a homotopy in the penalty weight, reconciles fit and selection, with a local convergence guarantee. In experiments, it recovers the parameters on long records of expanding and chaotic systems on which single shooting fails.
Systems and Control.comment: Preprint submitted to IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control

Systems and Control.title: Passive iFIR filters for data-driven velocity control in robotics
Systems and Control.summary: We present a passive, data-driven velocity control method for nonlinear robotic manipulators that achieves better tracking performance than optimized PID with comparable design complexity. Using only three minutes of probing data, a VRFT-based design identifies passive iFIR controllers that (i) preserve closed-loop stability via passivity constraints and (ii) outperform a VRFT-tuned PID baseline on the Franka Research 3 robot in both joint-space and Cartesian-space velocity control, achieving up to a 74.5% reduction in tracking error for the Cartesian velocity tracking experiment with the most demanding reference model. When the robot end-effector dynamics change, the controller can be re-learned from new data, regaining nominal performance. This study bridges learning-based control and stability-guaranteed design: passive iFIR learns from data while retaining passivity-based stability guarantees, unlike many learning-based approaches.

Systems and Control.title: Stability and periodic switching in feedback systems with sector-bounded hybrid integrators
Systems and Control.summary: We study stability of piecewise linear systems composed of the feedback interconnection of a linear time-invariant process and a sector-bounded hybrid integrator. Exploiting the observation that for such systems state-dependent switching sequences asymptotically exhibit periodic behaviour, we develop a spectral approach to stability analysis as an alternative to sufficient Lyapunov-based methods. We formulate a conjecture that asymptotic periodicity holds irrespective of the initial conditions and system stability, and provide a description of the limit system and propose an algorithm to obtain its parameters. We establish this rigorously for second-order linear-time invariant processes. Based on spectral properties of the resulting periodic limit system, we derive sufficient stability conditions. The results provide a novel viewpoint for accurate stability analysis of general state-based piecewise linear systems.

Systems and Control.title: Periodic robust robotic rock chop via virtual model control
Systems and Control.summary: Robotic cutting is a challenging, contact-rich manipulation task where the robot must simultaneously negotiate unknown object mechanics, large contact forces, and precise motion requirements. Our hypothesis is that this complexity can be alleviated through the design of a physically structured virtual-model controller that uses switched virtual mechanisms to generate a robust, rhythmic rock-chop motion for robotic cutting, without requiring pre-planned trajectories or precise environmental information. Motion is generated by the interaction between the environment, the robot's dynamics, and the virtual forces of the switching virtual mechanism, ultimately realized through the available actuation. Through theoretical and numerical analysis, together with experimental validation, we demonstrate that the controlled robot behavior settles into a stable periodic motion. Experiments with a Franka manipulator demonstrate robust cuts across five different vegetables, achieving sub-millimeter slice accuracy for thicknesses from 1 mm to 7 mm at a rate of nearly one cut per second. The controller maintains high performance despite changes in knife shape or cutting board height, and successfully adapts to a different humanoid manipulator, demonstrating robustness and platform independence.
Systems and Control.comment: Accepted for publication in The International Journal of Robotics Research

Systems and Control.title: Soft projections for robust data-driven control
Systems and Control.summary: We consider data-based predictive control based on behavioral systems theory. In the linear setting this means that a system is described as a subspace of trajectories, and predictive control can be formulated using a projection onto the intersection of this behavior and a constraint set. Instead of learning the model, or subspace, we focus on determining this projection from data. Motivated by the use of regularization in data-enabled predictive control (DeePC), we introduce the use of soft projections, which approximate the true projector onto the behavior from noisy data. In the simplest case, these are equivalent to known regularized DeePC schemes, but they exhibit a number of benefits. First, we provide a bound on the approximation error consisting of a bias and a variance term that can be traded-off by the regularization weight. The derived bound is independent of the true system order, highlighting the benefit of soft projections compared to low-dimensional subspace estimates. Moreover, soft projections allow for intuitive generalizations, one of which we show has superior performance on a case study. Finally, we provide update formulas for soft projectors enabling the efficient adaptation of the proposed data-driven control methods in the case of streaming data.

Systems and Control.title: Online outlier-resilient data-driven moving horizon estimation for linear discrete-time systems
Systems and Control.summary: This paper addresses data-driven state estimation for linear systems of which online output measurements may be corrupted by sparse outliers of arbitrary magnitude. Using only offline input-state-output data without explicitly identifying a system model, we propose an outlier-resilient data-driven moving horizon estimation scheme, termed OORD-MHE, based on Willems' fundamental lemma. The scheme employs a truncated-quadratic loss on the output residuals, parameterized by a truncation threshold, to mitigate the influence of online outliers. We establish sufficient conditions under which the resulting estimation error remains uniformly bounded. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed OORD-MHE scheme generates accurate state estimates in the presence of sparse online outliers.

Systems and Control.title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code
Systems and Control.summary: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define \emph{metadata-conditioned, import-level vendor--protocol incompatibility} and build \textsc{Proteus-OT}, a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character $n$-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.

Systems and Control.title: Damping Ratio and Convergence Rate Analysis for Inverter-Based Power Systems via Root Locus
Systems and Control.summary: As more renewables enter the grid, it becomes insufficient to rely solely on the center of inertia frequency to analyze the transient performance, especially for oscillation behaviors. Motivated by this, we study the transient frequency performance of inverter-based power systems. Two key performance criteria are considered: the damping ratio and the convergence rate, which are determined by the angles and the real parts of the closed-loop poles, respectively. By decomposing the network system into a set of scalar feedback systems, we show that the closed-loop poles can be analyzed using the root locus of a scalar feedback system as the gain varies from the smallest nonzero eigenvalue to the largest eigenvalue of the scaled Laplacian matrix of the interconnection network. Based on this, we derive sufficient conditions that ensure desired damping and convergence performance. Our analysis shows that the worst-case damping ratio and convergence rate occur when the gain equals the largest and the smallest nonzero eigenvalues of the scaled Laplacian, respectively. This result significantly simplifies the performance assessment. We further provide guidelines for tuning the inverter parameter. Numerical simulations are included to illustrate and validate the proposed approach.
Systems and Control.comment: This manuscript has been accepted by IFAC 2026

Systems and Control.title: Iterative Identification of Aperiodic Sampled-Data Systems via Affine LPV Models Scheduled by the Sampling Interval
Systems and Control.summary: This paper proposes a method for identifying a control-oriented model of a stable continuous-time linear system from aperiodically sampled input-output data. Rather than recovering the continuous-time matrices, the method directly identifies a discrete-time linear parameter-varying (LPV) state-space model that depends affinely on the measured normalized sampling-interval variation, a structure obtained from the first-order expansion of the zero-order-hold discretization. The resulting model is directly usable in control design for aperiodic sampled-data systems. An initial LPV estimate, including approximate first-order terms, is derived from a standard LTI subspace model through sampled-data relations. The method then iteratively alternates state-sequence reconstruction and LPV parameter refitting. Numerical examples show that the identified model retains high validation accuracy over a wide range of sampling-interval variations where a fixed LTI model degrades. Already at initialization, the state-space LPV structure substantially outperforms an LPV-ARX regression with the same scheduling variable, and the iterative refinement brings the model close to a state-measured benchmark, a practical upper-bound reference.
Systems and Control.comment: Submitted to Automatica

Systems and Control.title: From Rule-based to Agentic: LLM Agent based Real-time Control of Urban Drainage Systems for Flooding and Sewer Overflow Mitigation
Systems and Control.summary: Real-time control (RTC) for urban drainage systems (UDS) remains hampered by sparse in-network sensing. While heterogeneous multi-modal meteorological early warnings often contain decision-critical information for UDS RTC, none of the existing approaches can exploit such externally-sourced information within the control workflow. Here we introduce AgenticAI-Control, an agentic artificial intelligence framework able to assimilate multi-source meteorological early warnings in RTC. Two coupled large language model agents are integrated to generate control strategies by retrieving meteorological early-warnings and fusing them with domain engineering expertise. Validated via simulation studies of a combined sewer catchment in eastern China across 10 real-world rainfall events, the AgenticAI-Control achieved 69.1-90.6% reduction in aggregated flood and overflow volumes compared to the rule-based baseline control. Rigorously standardized prompt engineering and modular workflow constraints substantially compress performance disparities among four distinct LLMs. Our work establishes AgenticAI as a viable tool to unify multi-source meteorological monitoring and practitioner domain knowledge, surmounting longstanding monitoring limitations of UDS RTC and delivering cost-efficient, robust intelligent control solutions for sensor-sparse sewer infrastructures.

Systems and Control.title: Active road noise control using networked mean-square learning and lightweight conditional compensation experts
Systems and Control.summary: Multichannel active road noise control (ARNC) requires effective noise reduction (NR) under causality and computational constraints. A computationally efficient method is proposed that separates linear control from condition-dependent nonlinear residual compensation. A finite impulse response (FIR) baseline filter is obtained through networked mean-square learning that can be made adaptive, while a multi-resolution FIR mixture-of-experts (MRF-MoE) module provides possibly nonlinear corrections. Training comprises baseline initialization, sample-graph-regularized expert and router optimization, and joint refinement. Target channels are treated as nodes in a connected network for mean-square error minimization, whereas training windows define a graph for regularizing routing probabilities. Each expert combines short-time dense and long-tail low-rank FIR filtering, and causal single-expert routing reduces inference computation. Compared with WaveNet-VNN under the same configuration, the proposed method reduces estimated inference cost by 96.3% while achieving higher NR on the test set.

Systems and Control.title: A Note on Emergent Behavior in Multi-agent Systems Enabled by Neuro-spike Communication
Systems and Control.summary: In this note, we show emergent behavior can arise even when the agents interact solely through spikes. Rather than exchanging real-valued states, each agent encodes its own state by bio-inspired neuromorphic amplifiers and transmits signed spikes, so that each firing carries a single bit and the traffic is intermittent and asynchronous. We model the resulting network as a hybrid system and introduce a coordinate that is invariant under the spike-induced jumps, which reduces the convergence analysis to a flow dynamics without jumps. On this coordinate, we prove that the agents practically synchronize and collectively follow the blended dynamics that characterizes an emergent behavior, and we derive explicit ultimate error bounds for synchronization and for the expected behavior. The bound reveals a certified accuracy--threshold trade-off and yields closed-form tuning rules under a minimum-threshold or prescribed-accuracy constraints. A distributed median solver is tested using neuro-spike communication.

Systems and Control.title: Barrier-Based Safety Filtering for Quadrotor Flight in Cluttered Environments Under Acceleration Limits
Systems and Control.summary: Accurate trajectory tracking alone does not guarantee safe quadrotor flight when the reference passes near obstacles or the available control authority is limited. This paper presents a safety-filtered trajectory-tracking framework for a quadrotor operating at a fixed altitude in obstacle-cluttered environments. A nominal tracking controller is combined with high-order control barrier constraints and an acceleration-constrained quadratic program. The safety filter preserves the nominal acceleration whenever it is admissible and modifies it only when the prescribed obstacle clearance is threatened. The analysis establishes nominal exponential tracking, forward invariance of the safe region under compatible initial conditions and continued quadratic-program feasibility, and bounded tracking error during safety intervention. Numerical experiments using an idealized planar translational model with single and multiple stationary circular obstacles show minimum clearances of $0.000$--$0.001$~m under the safety filter, compared with $-1.594/-1.421$~m under nominal control. Tracking RMSE increases from $0.618$ to $0.950$~m across reference-speed scales $0.6$--$1.6$, illustrating the effect of reference speed on tracking accuracy under safety constraints. Additional tests examine how acceleration limits affect control effort and feasibility. These findings inform safety-filter design for UAV trajectory tracking under limited control authority.

Systems and Control.title: Loop-OPF: Solver-Informed Learning for Optimal Power Flow with Inference-Time Topology Adaptivity
Systems and Control.summary: Learning for optimal power flow (OPF) has recently been advocated to accelerate OPF solutions by using a pre-trained neural network (NN) to predict directly from given inputs such as the load demand. However, existing learning-for-OPF methods largely fall short of ensuring the optimality and feasibility of their predictions. They also struggle to adapt at inference time to unseen topology scenarios, such as those caused by line or generator outages. This work puts forth Loop-OPF, a solver-informed NN that builds its layers from the iterations of the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method. Under standard convexity and regularity conditions on DC-OPF, the resultant fixed-point output of Loop-OPF is thus optimal and feasible. To speed up PDHG across diverse OPF scenarios, Loop-OPF learns certain PDHG parameters in a self-supervised manner, without any OPF solution labels. We adopt the deep equilibrium (DEQ) framework for training so that the memory cost does not grow with the number of layers. As the grid topology enters every layer as an input, the same trained Loop-OPF directly adapts to unseen contingencies without retraining. Numerical tests on the IEEE 300-bus and PEGASE 1354-, 2869-, and 9241-bus networks have demonstrated the accuracy and topology adaptivity of the proposed Loop-OPF over competing learning-for-OPF methods.
Systems and Control.comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Preprint. Code: https://github.com/MFHChehade/loop-opf

Systems and Control.title: AdaPTwin: Adaptive Multi-Fidelity Predictive Digital Twin for Proactive Radio Resource Management in Vehicular Networks
Systems and Control.summary: The highly dynamic nature of vehicular networks necessitates proactive and site-specific radio resource management (RRM) for safety-critical services. While Network Digital Twins (NDTs) have emerged as a promising enabler, physics-based ray tracing is time-consuming, challenging accurate RRM under strict latency constraints. We propose AdaPTwin, an adaptive multi-fidelity predictive NDT framework for proactive and latency-aware RRM in vehicular networks. Unlike single- and multi-fidelity NDTs with fixed fidelity levels, AdaPTwin selects the NDT fidelity by constrained optimization under a per-slot latency budget. The framework adopts a hierarchical cloud-edge architecture: fidelity selection is performed periodically in the cloud, whereas the proactive RRM loop runs at the edge in every slot. The edge loop predicts the channels between vehicles and roadside units (RSUs) through trajectory forecasting, using a Transformer with continual learning, and look-ahead ray tracing with NVIDIA Sionna over a dynamically updated 3D scene of buildings, roads, and vehicles. A joint RSU beamforming and vehicle-RSU association problem is then solved to maximize the proportionally fair sum rate using a scalable multi-start iterative coordinate descent algorithm. AdaPTwin is assessed in a simulation-based evaluation in which a high-fidelity reference NDT, rather than field measurements, provides the accuracy reference. Comparisons with reactive, single-fidelity, and non-adaptive predictive NDTs and the stochastic 3GPP model show that AdaPTwin adapts to the evaluated traffic densities and urban layouts, where fixed-fidelity DT frameworks either lose accuracy or overrun their deadline. In the evaluated scenarios, AdaPTwin achieves up to 70% sum-rate gain and 80% outage probability reduction compared with a non-adaptive predictive multi-fidelity NDT while meeting the per-slot deadline.
Systems and Control.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

Systems and Control.title: Experiment-as-Code Labs: A Declarative Stack for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
Systems and Control.summary:
To unleash the full potential of AI for Science, we must untether the agents from a purely digital environment. The agent's ability to control and explore in real-world labs is essential because the physical lab remains foundational to scientific discovery. While some tasks can be performed on a computer (e.g., data analysis, running simulated experiments), Eureka moments could occur at any time while operating lab instruments (e.g., when a scientist notices unexpected clues, intuition may prompt a real-time course change). Although autonomous labs are on the rise, which expose programmable APIs to control scientific instruments via software, bridging the gap between increasingly powerful AI agents and automated lab equipment requires innovation that draws insights from computer systems.
  We propose a new paradigm called ``Experiment-as-Code (EaC) Labs,'' where a core concept is to encode experiments as declarative configurations that can be compiled down to device-level APIs. AI agents come up with hypotheses and experiments, written as an ensemble of declarative configurations. The systems layer performs program analysis, safety checks, resource assignment, and job orchestration. Finally, programmatic experimentation occurs via actuating the device APIs. This is a general stack that is science-, lab-, and instrument-independent, representing a novel synthesis across the physical, systems, and intelligence layers to unleash the next breakthrough in AI for Science.
Systems and Control.comment: Experiment-as-Code (EaC) white paper

Systems and Control.title: Federated Policy Gradient for Dynamic Consensus: Gradient Dominance and Topological Bounds
Systems and Control.summary: This paper presents a federated optimization framework for dynamic consensus in homogeneous multi-agent systems. The underlying problem is challenged by the communication graph's spectral properties, which induce spatial heterogeneity and complicate decentralized control even when the dynamics of the agents are completely known. The problem is addressed in this paper by bridging distributed control theory with federated policy gradients. Accordingly, a comprehensive optimization landscape for dynamic consensus is established through a modal decomposition formulation. Specifically, a parameterized suboptimality bound is characterized that explicitly decouples the true aggregate policy gradient from the network covariance mismatch. Building on this formulation, sufficient conditions based on the graph's Laplacian spectrum are derived to recover exact gradient dominance, which guarantees convergence to the global consensus policy and establishes a lower bound on the achievable dominance coefficient. Furthermore, a Federated model-free consensus algorithm is proposed that utilizes zeroth-order exploration alongside a bisection-based discount factor annealing mechanism, successfully eliminating the need for an initial stabilizing policy. This approach achieves linear global convergence for policy optimization subroutines while maintaining strictly bounded outer iterations until dynamic consensus is achieved. Through extensive simulation studies and comparative feasibility analyses across diverse network topologies, it is demonstrated that the proposed federated approach consistently outperforms existing model-based and data-driven separation-based techniques.

Systems and Control.title: Frequency-Structured Hamiltonian Neural Network for Multi-Timescale Dynamics
Systems and Control.summary: Learning coupled fast and slow dynamics accurately remains challenging for structure-preserving neural models. Hamiltonian Neural Networks preserve a learned Hamiltonian, but their neural parameterizations are susceptible to spectral bias, which favors slowly varying components and can leave fast oscillations poorly resolved. We introduce the Frequency-Structured Hamiltonian Neural Network (FS-HNN), which organizes Hamiltonian learning across temporal frequency scales. FS-HNN learns Hamiltonian components from frequency-filtered views of observed trajectories and combines them nonlinearly into a single scalar Hamiltonian. This enables the model to represent interactions across timescales while conserving the learned energy in continuous time. For PDEs, FS-HNN represents Hamiltonian components as neural functionals and learns a spatial operator, using orthogonal projection to conserve the learned energy. Experiments on ODE and PDE benchmarks spanning nonlinear oscillators, coupled lattices, shallow water flows, and dispersive waves show that FS-HNN improves long-horizon rollout accuracy over existing baselines, with accompanying gains in physical-energy fidelity.

Systems and Control.title: Gaussian Process Data-Driven Hamiltonian for Probabilistic Safe Set Construction
Systems and Control.summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability is a general framework for verifying the safety of nonlinear systems, but it relies on an accurate dynamics model. The data-driven Hamiltonian (DDH) framework avoids system identification by lower-bounding the Hamiltonian directly from state-control-velocity data. However, it requires a Lipschitz bound on the unknown dynamics which is hard to certify from finite data, and as a single global constant this bound makes the computed safe sets conservative. We propose the Gaussian process data-driven Hamiltonian (GP-DDH), a fully data-driven framework that constructs safe sets with probabilistic guarantees under a GP prior on the dynamics. Furthermore, we suggest two methods to choose the confidence parameter $β$, both mathematically guaranteed to underbound the Hamiltonian. The computed safe set lies inside the true one with posterior probability at least $1-Δ$ for any $Δ\in(0,1)$. Numerical experiments show that GP-DDH recovers a bigger volume of the true safe set than DDH while still correctly providing a conservative approximation, even when DDH is given a Lipschitz constant computed from the true dynamics.
Systems and Control.comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 9th Annual Learning for Dynamics and Control Conference (L4DC 2027)

Systems and Control.title: GreenDynaMix: Thermal-Aware Dynamic Mixed-Precision MoE LLM Inference Systems
Systems and Control.summary: Sustained Large Language Model (LLM) inference generates significant heat that exacerbates silicon aging and reduces GPU reliability. Because GPU temperature fluctuates continuously with workload intensity and ambient conditions, keeping it in a safe range requires real-time frequency scaling, which inevitably comes at the cost of either throughput or accuracy. To address this tightly coupled challenge, we propose GreenDynaMix, the first runtime system to jointly integrate a DVFS-based thermal manager with a dynamic precision-tuning throughput compensator. A sensitivity-aware allocator leverages intrinsic importance signals from the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router to assign higher precision to critical experts, preserving accuracy. Experiments on server, desktop, and embedded platforms demonstrate that GreenDynaMix reduces the temperature-induced aging rate of GPUs during LLM inference by 25-33%. Without offline profiling or model retraining, it recovers throughput at a perplexity cost of 0.9-1.6% with 8-bit/4-bit mixed precision, rising to 9.4% where memory forces 4-bit/2-bit.

Systems and Control.title: DAA for an Autonomous Delivery Drone: Maneuver Selection Policies for Near-Collision Risk Avoidance
Systems and Control.summary:
Detect-and-avoid (DAA) systems for autonomous drones operating in shared airspace must select avoidance maneuvers under conditions that differ markedly from those assumed by conventional DAA architectures designed for crewed aircraft. Limited on-board sensing capabilities restrict detection of collision risk to near distances (sub-km), the time available for decision-making is severely limited, uncertainty in the predicted closest point of approach (CPA) and the time to reach it is substantial, and the maneuver envelope of a small uncrewed aircraft at low altitude is tightly constrained.
  This paper presents and compares two maneuver-selection strategies that address these challenges: (1) a purely geometric approach, steering in the direction away from the intruder at CPA, and (2) a method that also takes into account the known sources of uncertainty in the intruder's location, and steers away from a plane expected to contain the intruder's location distribution at CPA.
  Performance is evaluated using the risk ratio metric on a large dataset of simulated near-collision encounters with crewed intruders. Results indicate that both strategies are feasible (i.e., computable in closed form from an onboard track estimate), and that the second strategy substantially outperforms the first.
Systems and Control.comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, accepted for publication at AIAA SciTech Forum 2027, Orlando FL, Jan 11-15 2027

Logic in Computer Science.title: Approximate Counting and the Provability of Combinatorial Principles
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Understanding which axioms suffice for the provability of known results in algorithms and complexity and whether they can settle longstanding conjectures in these areas is a fundamental direction at the intersection of logic and computer science. Motivated by this research program and its applications, we investigate bounded arithmetic theories designed to serve as a logical foundation for *probabilistic reasoning*, the relation between these theories, and whether they can prove more theorems than their underlying base theory for *deterministic reasoning*.
  In more detail, for nearly twenty years, Jeřábek's theory $\mathsf{APC}_1$ [Jeř07a] has provided a standard framework for the formalization of results from theoretical computer science relying on probabilistic techniques. In a recent work, [CLOW26] introduced a (possibly weaker) theory called $\mathsf{APX}_1$. This theory is able to capture a large set of probabilistic arguments using four simple axioms for *approximate counting*. Both theories extend Cook's theory $\mathsf{PV}_1$ [Coo75] for deterministic polynomial-time reasoning.
  Our main result establishes that, in the relativized setting, $\mathsf{APX}_1$ does not prove the retraction weak pigeonhole principle ($\mathsf{rwPHP}$). Consequently, $\mathsf{APC}_1$ is not conservative over $\mathsf{APX}_1$ with respect to relativized $\forallΣ^b_1$ sentences. Moreover, we establish that the unprovability of $\mathsf{rwPHP}$ is part of a more general phenomenon: for a large class of finite combinatorial principles, the existence of an *infinite model* of the negation of the principle *characterizes* its unprovability in $\mathsf{APX}_1$. This result, which is analogous to a theorem of Riis [Rii94], implies that $\mathsf{PV}_1$ and $\mathsf{APX}_1$ prove exactly the same finite combinatorial principles of this form.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Procedurally generated logic problems are used to both evaluate and train reasoning in language models. Their difficulty is usually set by planting a proof, that is, by sampling a proof of the desired depth and stating its premises as the problem. However, a planted proof is only one possible proof. A problem can also have shorter proofs, or several unrelated ones, and its stated depth then overstates what solving it requires. We measure what a problem actually requires, relative to a stated set of inference rules. For each problem, we compute the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs and the indispensable premises, and export certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find depth that is forced (ProofWriter, Blocksworld), problems labelled depth 5 that require about two specific rule applications (FLDx2), and answers that need no particular step (ZebraLogic). We then construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, using a catalog of shortcuts proved once per rule set. Every constructed problem is checked in full and comes with its own certificate. In training, the best data mixes depths and problem types. At equal size, such mixtures of certified problem types, including model-checking problems that forward generation does not produce, transfer better than FLDx2-style derivation data for Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 24 pages, 5 figures. Code/data: https://github.com/sileod/semforge

Logic in Computer Science.title: FOL-Proof: Verifying LLM Text-to-Logic Translations via Deterministic Semantics
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.

Logic in Computer Science.title: On Presburger Arithmetic Expanded with Prime Numbers
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We prove unconditionally that the first-order theory of Presburger arithmetic expanded by a predicate for the primes is undecidable. Bateman, Jockusch and Woods proved this in 1993 assuming Dickson's conjecture. We use the counter-machine framework of Karimov, Nieuwveld and Ouaknine and their idea of using `arbitrary permutations', and the number-theoretic input comes from Hildebrand and Maier's 1988 proof that the limit points of $k$ consecutive normalised prime gaps have positive measure. We use a discrete version, which they obtain before limits are taken. The key lemma is that although Hildebrand and Maier's result does not seem to give arbitrary permutations of consecutive prime gaps, it gives arbitrary permutations for the differences $p_i - q_i$ for two finite blocks of consecutive primes $p_0 < \cdots < p_k$ and $q_0 < \cdots < q_k$. Moreover, with the same key lemma, we show that Presburger arithmetic expanded with the function that maps $n$ to the $n$th prime defines multiplication.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Counting on Nowhere Dense Classes
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We establish an algorithmic framework for query answering and enumeration in first-order logic with counting on effectively nowhere dense classes of relational structures. Our main technical contribution is an algorithm that, after almost-linear-time preprocessing on a structure $A$ from such a class and a first-order formula $φ(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, can answer the following queries in constant time: given a tuple $\bar{v} \in A^{|\bar{x}|}$, output the number of tuples $\bar{w} \in A^{|\bar{y}|}$ satisfying $A \models φ(\bar{v},\bar{w})$. In database terms, this is constant-time evaluation of grouped counting queries. Building on this, we achieve constant-time query answering and constant-delay enumeration for the recently introduced clique-guarded first-order logic with counting (cgFOC) [van Bergerem, Lange, and Schweikardt, MFCS 2026] on effectively nowhere dense classes. These results unify and generalise previous work on nowhere dense classes, namely first-order testing and enumeration [Schweikardt, Segoufin, and Vigny, JACM 2022] and the evaluation of the counting logic FOC1 [Grohe and Schweikardt, PODS 2018]. Moreover, under the assumption $\mathrm{FPT} \neq \mathrm{AW}[*]$, our results are essentially optimal: they do not extend to subgraph-closed graph classes beyond the nowhere dense ones, slight generalisations of the clique-guarding mechanism are intractable even on very simple sparse classes, and very restricted fragments of cgFOC are already intractable on very simple dense classes.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 29 pages. Improved presentation and fixed an issue in the proof of Lemma 15 (previously Lemma 16)

Logic in Computer Science.title: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Accepted at the 28th International Conference on Distributed Computing and Networking (ICDCN 2027), Surathkal, India, January 4-7, 2027. 10 pages

Logic in Computer Science.title: Pushdown Reachability Requires $N^2$ Time on Multitape Turing Machines
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Pushdown reachability, or equivalently, language non-emptiness of pushdown automata (PDA), is a fundamental problem in automata theory and program analysis. We show that, for every $ε>0$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide pushdown reachability in $O(N^{2-ε})$ time, where $N$ is the input size. The lower bound already holds for \emph{sparse instances}, i.e., instances in which the number of transitions is linear in the number of states. This gives the first unconditional super-linear lower bound for pushdown reachability. Furthermore, we also extend this result and show that for any $ε> 0$ and $k \ge 1$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide the intersection non-emptiness problem of one PDA and $k-1$ NFAs in time $O(N^{2k-ε})$, where $N$ is the input size.
  Finally, pushdown reachability is well-known to be quasi-linear time equivalent to many different problems in program analysis. Our result translates to all of those problems as well and provides the first unconditional super-linear lower bounds for those problems on multitape Turing machines.

Logic in Computer Science.title: A Myhill-Nerode Theorem for Generalized Automata, with Applications to Pattern Matching and Compression
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
The model of generalized automata, introduced by Eilenberg in 1974, allows representing a regular language more concisely than conventional automata by allowing edges to be labeled not only with characters, but also strings. Giammarresi and Montalbano introduced a notion of determinism for generalized automata [STACS 1995]. While generalized deterministic automata retain many properties of conventional deterministic automata, the uniqueness of a minimal generalized deterministic automaton is lost.
  In the first part of the paper, we show that the lack of uniqueness can be explained by introducing a set $ \mathcal{W(A)} $ associated with a generalized automaton $ \mathcal{A} $. In this way, we derive for the first time a full Myhill-Nerode theorem for generalized automata, which contains the textbook Myhill-Nerode theorem for conventional automata as a degenerate case. In the second part of the paper, we show that the set $ \mathcal{W(A)} $ leads to applications for pattern matching and data compression. We show that a Wheeler generalized automata can be stored using $ \mathfrak{e} \log σ(1 + o(1)) + O(e) $ bits so that pattern matching queries can be solved in $ O(m \log \log σ) $ time, where $ \mathfrak{e} $ is the total length of all edge labels, $ e $ is the number of edges, $ σ$ is the size of the alphabet and $ m $ is the length of the pattern.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Elementary first-order model checking for sparse graphs
Logic in Computer Science.summary: It is known that for subgraph-closed graph classes the first-order model checking problem is fixed-parameter tractable if and only if the class is nowhere dense [Grohe, Kreutzer, Siebertz, 2017]. However, the dependency on the formula size is non-elementary, and in fact, this is unavoidable even for the class of all trees [Frick and Grohe, 2004]. On the other hand, it is known that the dependency is elementary for classes of bounded degree [Frick and Grohe, 2004] as well as for classes of bounded pathwidth [Lampis, 2026]. In this paper we generalise these results and almost completely characterise subgraph-closed graph classes for which the model checking problem is fixed-parameter tractable with an elementary dependency on the formula size. Those are the graph classes for which there exists a number $d$ such that for every $r$, some tree of depth $d$ and size bounded by an elementary function of $r$ is avoided as an $(\le r)$-subdivision in all graphs in the class. In particular, this implies that if the class in question excludes a fixed tree as a topological minor, then first-order model checking for graphs in the class is fixed-parameter tractable with an elementary dependency on the formula size.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 57 pages. This is the TheoretiCS journal version

Logic in Computer Science.title: Further Comments on Yablo's Construction
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We continue our analysis of Yablo's coding of the liar paradox by infinite acyclic graphs. The present notes are based on and continue the author's previous results on the problem. In particular, our approach is often more systematic than before. We also show a representation result, and compare to work of other authors. NOTE: IF DIAGRAMS HAVE A PROBLEM IN THE PDF VERSION, PLEASE TRY THE HTML VERSION.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Concurrent Visibility: Higher-Order Concurrency with First-Order Store
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We propose an Operational Game Semantics for a (call-by-value) concurrent higher-order language with first-order store (references may contain other references or first-order values such as integers or booleans; however they may not store higher-order values such as functions). We adapt the game-semantic notion of visibility, which semantically captures the absence of higher-order references and developed for sequential higher-order languages, to a concurrent setting. We thus define a complete-trace preorder, and prove it sound for the contextual preorder, by introducing a synchronization-based composition of semantic configurations and establishing an observational adequacy result. We also prove completeness for the subset of the language in which functions return first-order values. In contrast to the case of sequential visibility, in the labeled transition semantics we have to account for the presence of multiple active threads with possibly different visibilities, and of a tree-like structure for managing the dependencies among the threads so created. Moreover, we have to reason on families of traces, rather than single traces, as in concurrent setting the order among certain actions cannot be enforced.

Logic in Computer Science.title: SAT Solving for Power Peak Minimization in the Parallel--Serial--with--Crossover Assembly Line Balancing Problem
Logic in Computer Science.summary: The Parallel--Serial-with-Crossover Assembly Line Balancing Problem with Power Peak Minimization (PSCALB3PM) was introduced by Delorme and Gianessi (2022), who proposed an integer linear programming (ILP) model, and further developed in 2024 with a multi-start local-search matheuristic. This paper presents an exact approach based on Boolean satisfiability (SAT) that combines a compact encoding with incremental SAT solving. Specifically, it develops a compact encoding of task-to-workstation precedence constraints and an incremental SAT-based optimization procedure for power peak minimization. We evaluate the proposed method on 375 benchmark instances and compare it with both reference methods. SAT finds feasible solutions for all 375 instances and certifies optimality for 159, compared with 346 feasible solutions and 126 optimality certificates obtained by the ILP method. Relative to the reference matheuristic, SAT achieves lower power peaks on 130 instances, whereas the matheuristic obtains lower values on only four. These findings establish SAT as a competitive exact method for PSCALB3PM, achieving higher feasible-solution coverage and more optimality proofs than the reference ILP model, while generally outperforming the existing matheuristic in terms of solution quality.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 30 pages, 7 figures

Logic in Computer Science.title: Self-Reference and Relative Incompleteness: From Logical Obstructions to Hardness Hypotheses
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
We define relative incompleteness and use it to provide a unified framework for Gödelian incompleteness and the limits of local observations in finite SAT. A background is incomplete relative to a target question if two realizations compatible with that background give opposite answers. Gödelian diagonalization yields a sentence whose truth value differs across two models of the same theory, while solution-dependent blocking yields two formulas that agree on the observed clauses but differ in satisfiability. Both constructions realize a common diagonal relation between truth and acceptance that forces a sound partial evaluator to leave the target undecided.
  For a satisfiable formula, replacing a single unobserved clause without changing its variable support can make the formula unsatisfiable exactly when all solutions remaining after deletion of that clause agree on its support. If the original formula has a unique solution, this condition is equivalent to redundancy of the clause. More generally, an observation of a satisfiable formula determines satisfiability exactly when it includes a position at which the formula differs from each unsatisfiable completion. For uniquely satisfiable formulas, the positions that every sufficient observation must include are precisely the redundant ones. We also arithmetize solution blocking and construct a tagged fixed point that refers to its own blocking data. Finally, we use self-referential $K$-SAT to illustrate how relative incompleteness can provide a logical foundation for formulating a quantitative hardness hypothesis.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 20 pages

Logic in Computer Science.title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Ranking functions are a fundamental technique for proving loop termination, but synthesizing them remains challenging and often requires substantial expertise. Despite considerable progress in their automated synthesis, existing approaches remain limited in their effectiveness. We propose RAINFALL, a neuro-symbolic framework that tightly integrates large language models (LLMs) with symbolic verification. To our best knowledge, RAINFALL is the first to employ a generate-verify-refine paradigm for LLM-based ranking function synthesis. RAINFALL formulates ranking function synthesis as a constrained code-completion task, inserting placeholders into the input program that the LLM must fill in four predefined slots per loop. The resulting program is checked by a symbolic verifier. Successful verification yields a valid ranking function, while verification failures produce diagnostics that are translated into natural-language feedback to guide iterative refinement. We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites comprising 358 terminating C programs. Using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, RAINFALL synthesizes verified ranking functions for 333 programs (93.02%), outperforming all evaluated baselines. Notably, it solves 22 more programs than PROTON 2.1, the winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination Category. Combining RAINFALL with PROTON 2.1 further increases the success rate to 96.65% (346/358 programs). Ablation studies demonstrate the contributions of placeholder contracts, few-shot examples, symbolic verification, and diagnostic feedback, while experiments across different LLMs establish the broader applicability of the framework.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 14 pages, 5 figures

Logic in Computer Science.title: No free lattice contains an infinite ascending chain of copies of FL(3)
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
No free lattice contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of sublattices isomorphic to FL(3), the free lattice on three generators; this answers a question that R. A. Dean asked and the second author's 1997 notes on the problem left open. Every such chain would yield, inside FL(3), a coherent chain of proper self-embeddings $Θ_0, Θ_1, Θ_2, \dots$ with $Θ_k \circ Θ_j = Θ_j$ for $j < k$, so that each later embedding fixes the image of each earlier one pointwise. Every proper self-embedding of FL(3) whose fixed sublattice contains a free generating triple fixes one of the three generators, say $z$, because a power of it or of its dual lies above the identity, and a self-embedding that moves every generator and lies above the identity fixes at most eleven elements. Up to duality, a proper self-embedding fixing the image of such a $Θ_1$ pointwise fixes only elements above $z \wedge (x \vee y)$, where no free generating triple containing $z$ can lie. We also verify the one-step example of the 1997 notes, prove that no step toward such a chain is self-similar, and show that the configuration the argument rules out at length three does occur at length two.
  Without freeness the answer reverses: FL(3) contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of 3-generated sublattices, so the lattice analogue of Takahasi's chain condition for free groups fails. The theorem itself is checked by the Agda proof assistant under its safe flags, for free lattices over generators with decidable equality, and its formal proof uses no classical principle: finite searches and an induction on a finite set replace the infinite pigeonhole principle by which a chain yields a coherent chain.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 60 pages, 13 figures. The main theorem is checked in Agda; the formal development is https://github.com/ualib/agda-deans-problem at its tag v0.1.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24375155. v2: footnotes and a reference added; the formal development cited at its tag

Logic in Computer Science.title: How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We now live in the age of machine-generated mathematics: AI systems produce research-level proofs faster than the human mathematical community can read them. Verification is only part of the challenge. We also need to know whether a "new proof" is indeed new, whether a thousand generated proofs contain one idea or many, and where each sits relative to human mathematics. All of these require measuring distances between proofs. Following Hilbert's 24th problem and the identity-of-proofs problem, we ask how far apart two proofs of one theorem are, and what shape the proof space they inhabit has. We define 19 dissimilarity measures in 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties, which we argue are the conditions for safely optimising a measure. In a Curry-Howard kernel, 5 machine-checked proofs that the primes are infinite show that raw syntax cannot tell a rewrite from a new argument, that dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), and that semantic measures invert it: Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. A replication in Lean 4/Mathlib (3 theorems, 19 proofs, 18 measures) confirms that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, and shows that equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, that proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and that proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs. We argue for reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile, extend the measures to proofs of different theorems, and discuss uses, from detecting duplicated AI proofs and orchestrating prover agents to interpreting AI proofs via their nearest human-understandable counterparts. Code, Lean sources and data are released.

Signal Processing.title: A concave-convex approach to bit depth allocation for linear MMSE estimation in wireless sensor networks with correlated noise
Signal Processing.summary: Nodes in a wireless sensor network (WSN) are generally powered by batteries, and therefore energy efficiency is crucial. The bit depth used to quantize the sensor signal samples heavily influences energy consumption, as it strongly impacts the amount of information to be transmitted between the sensor nodes. Bit depth allocation problems seek to assign a bit depth to each sensor signal to optimize network resources, such as energy or bandwidth, together with algorithmic performance. We study a general bit depth allocation problem for linear minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimation in WSNs with spatially correlated noise and a communication energy model depending linearly on the sensor bit depths. This model follows from common configurations in digital communications with orthogonal multiple-access schemes. After relaxation to real variables, we formulate the resulting non-convex problem as a difference of convex (DC) problem, and develop an algorithm based on the concave-convex procedure (CCP) to find a local optimum. We show that the convex problem involved in each CCP iteration can be efficiently solved with a worst-case complexity that is linear in the number of sensors. Additionally, we show that our approach is more computationally efficient than previously proposed bit depth allocation algorithms and generic optimization methods, and it achieves significant energy savings.
Signal Processing.comment: 16 pages double column, 10 figures

Signal Processing.title: MSW: a Multi-Scale Sliced Wasserstein Distance Between Image Distributions
Signal Processing.summary: We propose the multi-scale sliced Wasserstein (MSW) distance between image distributions, which operates in pixel space and requires no trained network. MSW convolves images with a fixed bank of discrete cosine filters at several scales, pools the responses over all positions, and compares the resulting one-dimensional distributions using the Wasserstein distance. We pair MSW with an exact two-sample test that gives calibrated p-values. Most metrics compare two image sets in the latent space of a pretrained network. We show that these metrics are insensitive to simple perturbations of the images, because the latent space is nearly invariant to them. In contrast, MSW detects smaller perturbations than latent-space metrics and needs far fewer images to do so. Although it uses no learned features, it still detects semantic changes of the image distribution. Finally, MSW matches or outperforms existing Wasserstein-based metrics in our experiments.

Signal Processing.title: Sensor-Stack Limits on Contactless In-Bed Body Position: A 20-Subject Multimodal Radar + Thermal LOSO Characterization
Signal Processing.summary: Contactless in-bed body-position inference can be limited by the sensor representation the host receives rather than by the classifier. We characterize a bedside 60 GHz frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar that reports only on-device constant-false-alarm-rate (CFAR) point clouds, together with a low-resolution thermal array (24x32 nominal, 24x16 effective), on 20 subjects under leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation. Two tasks share the cohort: 273 operator-directed in-bed posture holds (148.7 minutes) and a per-second bed-presence timeline (8,817 scored seconds). The cohort is a friends-and-family convenience sample (13 minors, ages 5 to 68, six families), and every session used the same bed in one room with the subject uncovered, so the figures describe this setup rather than a population. Bed presence reaches a 0.871 per-subject median balanced accuracy (95% CI 0.796 to 0.910). For four-class posture, nested LOSO, in which every selection and fitting step sees training subjects only, gives 0.646 balanced accuracy (per-subject median 0.683). Prone recall is 0.45 at a precision of 0.42, so prone is not usefully detected. Version 1 reported 0.674 for a stacked ensemble picked on the folds it was scored on; this version replaces that figure with a nested estimate and corrects the bed-presence accounting and the description of the recording setting. Thermal resolves left versus right (lateral swaps of 35 to 42% with radar alone, 8% with thermal alone). The supine-versus-prone breathing cue shows up in the CFAR output only as a group shift (Cohen's d = 0.61), with a clean per-hold peak in 8.4% of holds. The next hardware test is raw range-FFT access, not further classifier tuning on CFAR detections.

Signal Processing.title: InterGS+: Inter-Frame Gaussian Splatting Compression with Geometry-Aware Transformer Prediction and Adaptive Residual Coding
Signal Processing.summary: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides real-time photorealistic rendering, but representing each frame as irregular Gaussian primitives with high-dimensional attributes creates substantial storage and transmission cost. Exploiting temporal redundancy is challenging because Gaussian primitives do not preserve fixed identities across frames. We propose InterGS+, a lightweight post-hoc inter-frame codec that jointly improves temporal prediction and residual representation. Current-frame geometry is coded with G-PCC and reconstructed before prediction, enabling consistent temporal neighborhoods at encoder and decoder. Attributes are predicted using lightweight KNN and bilateral predictors together with a geometry-aware transformer for spherical-harmonic (SH) appearance, with per-Gaussian mode selection. Residual coding is adapted to each attribute: SH innovations are coded in a shared PCA domain using vector quantization with refinement, opacity and scale in activated gamma-companded domains, and rotation as canonicalized quaternion innovations using vector quantization and refinement. On MPEG dynamic sequences, InterGS+ achieves average BD-rate reductions of 45.48% over G-PCC Amd. 1 and 7.78% over InterGS-Lite, with corresponding BD-PSNR gains of 9.98 dB and 1.10 dB. Average decoding complexity is 0.049 ms/Gaussian, demonstrating efficient streamable dynamic 3DGS compression.
Signal Processing.comment: Accepted for poster presentation at the 2027 Data Compression Conference (DCC 2027)

Signal Processing.title: Directed brain-body graphs across timescales
Signal Processing.summary: Simultaneous brain and body recordings combine signals sampled at very different rates with processes that act on timescales from milliseconds to minutes. Placing all signals on one time grid can distort the directed relationships estimated from them. Unmeasured common influences can also make one signal appear to drive another. We introduce rate-matched Granger causality (RMGC), which estimates directed predictive relationships without a common sampling grid. Each relationship receives a robustness value, the strength of the weakest common influence found within a specified class that can reproduce it. A neural extension tests for nonlinear relationships. In a controlled benchmark, RMGC recovered more true relationships than four established methods and an autoregressive model on a common grid (92\% at a false-positive rate of 5\%). Given the same signal features, the common-grid model matched this recovery but had more than twice the false-positive rate, and it reversed the relationship from respiration to heart rate. The robustness value never overstated the strength of the driver behind a spurious relationship, even for drivers outside the searched class. It separated true from spurious relationships better than predictive strength did. In overnight sleep recordings and two awake datasets, many brain--heart relationships could be reproduced by common drivers no stronger than measured respiration. Robustness values only partly identified those that appeared when respiration was omitted, particularly during wakefulness. Surrogate analyses showed elevated background rates in one awake dataset. The approach applies to other signals recorded at different rates or as events, provided that influences act with a delay.

Signal Processing.title: Adaptive Microwave Reception with Diamond Spin Sensors
Signal Processing.summary: In a diamond-spin microwave receiver, pilot measurements can identify the spin-control phase that best separates binary phase-shift keyed symbols. Applying that phase takes time, during which carrier drift can erase the gain in alignment. We derive an exact feedback-delay threshold for a single payload spin from the phase information in the pilot record. On a finite menu of control phases, the pilot record enters the minimum-error update decision only through the direction of its first circular moment when that moment is nonzero. This result motivates a controller that estimates the direction from orthogonal pilot measurements and retains the existing phase whenever the predicted gain is lost to diffusion. For finite spin ensembles, we bound the distinguishability of the photon-count distributions in terms of optical readout and carrier-phase uncertainty, including fluctuations shared across spins. Packet simulations at matched spin budgets show that gated feedback can improve reliability with a single readout channel. With independently readable quadratures and sufficient spin preparations, decision-directed software tracking achieves lower packet error without a hardware phase update.

Signal Processing.title: Adaptive Beamforming Using One-Bit Data Samples for Covariance Estimation
Signal Processing.summary: The use of one-bit quantized complex-valued data samples enables efficient distributed computation of an array data covariance. This reduced complexity covariance estimate can be used for adaptive beamforming, but requires careful diagonal loading and results in lower performance compared to a full-precision approach. Two main approaches are presented: a covariance matrix built out of complex one-bit data samples, and a ``hybrid'' cross-covariance between the one-bit data and the full precision data. Signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) estimates for the associated population and finite-sample matrices are derived and compared to the full precision results using tools from linear algebra and statistics. Many strong, well-separated interferers with low overlap with the signal of interest are assumed throughout, none of them dominant.

Signal Processing.title: Goal-Oriented Wave Computing for Direction-of-Arrival Estimation
Signal Processing.summary: Programmable metasurfaces are arrays of elements whose electromagnetic response can be tuned electronically. They can process signals as a wave propagates through or reflects off them, an approach known as wave-domain analog computing, or wave computing. The design strategy is typically indirect: the surface is fitted to a prescribed linear operator, such as a discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and the result is read from output power measurements. Using direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation as a canonical benchmark, we study what this indirection costs across three analog computing topologies: reflective reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), beyond-diagonal RIS (BD-RIS), and stacked intelligent metasurfaces (SIM). We first derive Cramér-Rao bounds for the complete physical estimation chain, including one that accounts for output detectors measuring only intensity. We then formulate a goal-oriented alternative where the surfaces are trained directly through the deployed readout, with no operator target. We observe that goal-oriented training lets sparsely connected or shallower surfaces reach the task performance of their more complex operator-fitted counterparts, despite nearly identical Fisher information. For fully connected BD-RIS and six-layer SIM, the advantage persists under one- and two-bit control. From 16 to 64 elements, the connectivity a beyond-diagonal RIS needs grows with the aperture, and the depth saving of a stacked intelligent metasurface shrinks. Under tuner and per-layer loss, the goal-oriented designs mostly keep their advantage over DFT fits of the same hardware.
Signal Processing.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. v2: Monte Carlo results re-run with 60,000 trials; corrected quantized-control training and results; loss study with noise at the detectors; clarified scope; small corrections in the text and Table I

Signal Processing.title: Black-Box Comparator-Adaptive Network Regret
Signal Processing.summary: We study comparator-adaptive decentralized online learning with network regret, which evaluates each node's prediction on the loss of every node in the network. We show that existing gossip-based algorithms are fundamentally limited for this task, and cannot achieve sublinear network regret with only one gossip step per decision round. To prove this, we construct a two-node counterexample, which shows that gossip-based algorithms can produce exponential regret despite bounded disagreement, resolving a previously open question in the literature. We then introduce a black-box reduction, which uses local learners with sublinear comparator-adaptive regret to obtain sublinear comparator-adaptive network regret. Each node exchanges predictions with its neighbors once per decision round, and a universal choice of edge weights works on every connected undirected graph without graph preprocessing. We also characterize admissible edge weights and show how weights adapted to the graph improve the regret bound. For example, for the complete graph, this improvement is quadratic in the number of nodes. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data illustrate the counterexamples we propose and compare the reduction with decentralized baselines.

Signal Processing.title: Sheaf-Based Federated Representation Learning
Signal Processing.summary: Heterogeneous federated systems require agents to learn and exchange informative representations despite differences in data distributions, model architectures, and latent dimensionalities. We propose Sheaf-based Federated Representation Learning (SFRL), a framework that jointly learns and aligns heterogeneous latent representations without sharing parameters, labels, or a single latent space. SFRL relates agent-specific latent spaces through learnable orthogonal transformations and isometric embeddings, promoting consistency via a sheaf-Laplacian gluing regularizer evaluated on a shared set of pilot samples. We develop Sheaf-FRL, a decentralized alternating algorithm combining local gradient updates with closed-form Procrustes updates of the alignment maps, and establish convergence guarantees in deterministic and stochastic settings. On collaborative classification with semantic communication across four datasets, under model and data heterogeneity, Sheaf-FRL improves communication accuracy over federated baselines at no cost in private accuracy, and is more robust to latent-space compression.

Signal Processing.title: Enhancing time-frequency resolution with optimal transport and barycentric fusion of multiple spectrogram
Signal Processing.summary: Time-frequency representations, such as the short-time Fourier transform (STFT), are fundamental tools for analyzing non-stationary signals. However, their ability to achieve sharp localization in both time and frequency is inherently limited by the Gabor-Heisenberg uncertainty principle. In this paper, we address this limitation by introducing a method to generate super-resolution spectrograms through the fusion of two or more spectrograms with varying resolutions. Specifically, we compute the super-resolution spectrogram as the barycenter of input spectrograms using optimal transport (OT) divergences. Our method does not require the input spectrograms to share the same time-frequency grid. The input spectrograms can be computed using any STFT parameters, and the resulting super-resolution spectrogram can be defined on an arbitrary user-specified grid. We explore various OT divergences based on different transportation costs. Notably, we introduce a novel transportation cost that preserves time-frequency geometry while significantly reducing computational complexity compared to standard Wasserstein barycenters. We adopt the unbalanced OT framework and derive a new block majorization-minimization algorithm for efficient barycenter computation. We validate the proposed method on controlled synthetic signals and recorded speech using both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. The results show that our approach combines the best localization properties of the input spectrograms while maintaining a smooth energy distribution, and preserving computational efficiency.
Signal Processing.comment: main text: 15 pages, 5 figures. supplementary material: 4 pages, 4 figures

Signal Processing.title: From Points to Trajectories: Rethinking Multimodal Alignment for Physical Events
Signal Processing.summary: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate twin events from pooled features alone. Instead, we show that physical events are uniquely identified by the event gap, namely the instantaneous, synchronous co-fluctuations across modalities that are erased by pooling and accumulate only along unpooled trajectories. To recover this signal, we introduce CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement. Integrated across four state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment, consistently outperforming existing temporal alignment methods.

Signal Processing.title: A Closed-Loop Thermal Dynamic Model for AI Data Center Cooling Load Simulation
Signal Processing.summary: Accurate modeling and simulation of cooling electricity demand is essential for characterizing AI data center loads, but time-synchronized operational measurements are scarce. Constant coefficient-of-performance models can oversimplify cooling behavior, while detailed thermal state-space models are cumbersome to use. This paper proposes a closed-loop simulation framework that couples a linear thermal dynamic model with deadband-based control to capture nonlinear cooling behaviors. The framework is validated against operational data from the Marconi100 supercomputer. Compared with the baseline, the proposed model reduces the mean absolute error from 95.80 to 23.52 kW and the root-mean-square error from 109.79 to 29.91 kW. The statistical evaluation further shows improved reproduction of daily peak demand and intraday variability. The framework provides a computationally tractable approach to generate physically interpretable cooling load profiles for power system studies.

Signal Processing.title: PPGFlowECG: Latent Rectified Flow with Cross-Modal Encoding for PPG-Guided ECG Generation and Cardiovascular Disease Detection
Signal Processing.summary: Electrocardiography (ECG) is the clinical gold standard for cardiovascular disease (CVD) assessment, yet continuous monitoring is constrained by the need for dedicated hardware and trained personnel. Photoplethysmography (PPG) is ubiquitous in wearable devices and readily scalable, but it lacks electrophysiological specificity, limiting diagnostic reliability. While generative methods aim to translate PPG into clinically useful ECG signals, existing approaches are limited by the misalignment of physiological semantics in generative models and the complexity of modeling in high-dimensional signals. To address these limitations, we propose PPGFlowECG, a two-stage framework that aligns PPG and ECG in a shared latent space using the CardioAlign Encoder and then synthesizes ECGs with latent rectified flow. We further provide a formal analysis of this coupling, showing that the CardioAlign Encoder is necessary to guarantee stable and semantically consistent ECG synthesis under our formulation. Extensive experiments on four datasets demonstrate improved synthesis fidelity and downstream diagnostic utility. These results indicate that PPGFlowECG supports scalable, wearable-first CVD screening when standard ECG acquisition is unavailable.
Signal Processing.comment: Accepted at IEEE ICDM 2026 and awarded the Best Paper Award (Applied Track)

Signal Processing.title: The generalized method of moments is (almost) statistically efficient in low-SNR Gaussian latent-variable models
Signal Processing.summary: We study estimation in the low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regime for a broad class of Gaussian latent-variable models, including Gaussian mixtures and orbit-recovery problems. We show that, in this regime, the generalized method-of-moments (GMoM) matches the first-order asymptotic efficiency of maximum likelihood. In particular, if the moment features are chosen up to the minimal local order required for identification and are weighted optimally, then the resulting GMoM estimator has the same leading asymptotic covariance as the maximum-likelihood estimator. We further show that this efficiency can be achieved using practical, data-driven weighting schemes and is preserved under a broad class of simpler weighting choices, including the commonly used identity-weighted method of moments, although these may incur larger higher-order efficiency losses. On the other hand, inappropriate weighting or discarding moment entries can lead to persistent efficiency losses even as SNR tends to zero, despite preserving identifiability. These results distinguish the moments required for identifiability from those needed for statistical efficiency, and characterize when moment-based estimation can match the performance of maximum likelihood.

Signal Processing.title: A Proposal for Multiplierless RLS Adaptive Filters with Implementation Complexity Constraint
Signal Processing.summary: The so-called sum-of-powers-of-two arithmetic has the advantage of using simple shift and thus avoiding multiplications operations. In this work, we provide a feasible RLS adaptive filter algorithm employing the SOPOT representation. This reduces the computational burden of the RLS algorithm. Therefore, leading to a reduction in the power consumption from a hardware implementation point of view, which is an important feature in the developing of smaller, lighter and more power-efficient portable devices.

Signal Processing.title: Optimal Window Design for Intercarrier and Intersymbol Interference Power Minimization in w-OFDM
Signal Processing.summary: Block transceivers are essential for modern communication systems, and they are vastly implemented in many day-to-day devices, especially the orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) technique. The application of a pulseshaping technique in the OFDM generates the so-called windowed OFDM (w-OFDM). This letter proposes an optimization of the window shape, obtaining minimal intercarrier and intersymbol interference power, ICI, and ISI, respectively. A communication system is simulated by implementing the optimized w-OFDM, and its performance is compared with a non-optimized system using a raised-cosine window.

Signal Processing.title: Timestep Selection in Diffusion-Based OTFS Channel Estimation
Signal Processing.summary: Diffusion-based channel estimators are run with a few deterministic sampling steps, and their step count is treated as a knob that trades accuracy against latency. We show that for the mean squared error this trade-off mainly comes from the default leading timestep spacing, whose first timestep indicates an intermediate noise level although the initial state is pure noise. In a multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal time frequency space receiver with ray-traced paths and per-path Doppler shifts, moving only the first timestep of the default spacing to the pure-noise end recovers the gain of trailing spacing, completely for our anchored residual estimator and mostly for a published diffusion estimator. With trailing spacing one to three steps give the most accurate single trajectory of our estimator at every signal-to-noise ratio we test, and longer trajectories raise the error, by 0.34~dB over one step at a signal-to-noise ratio of 20~dB after 50 steps. This is the direction predicted by an idealized analysis in which a long deterministic trajectory turns the posterior mean into a posterior sample.
