In practice, the deployment of non-square uniform planar arrays (UPAs) fundamentally alters wavefront characteristics and induces anisotropic beamfocusing capability along different axes due to the aperture disparity originating from the non-square array geometry. To fully uncover the performance impact of such non-square geometry and thus unleash the potential of the non-square UPAs, we investigate the anisotropic near-field characteristics, fundamental limits, and channel estimation for non-square UPA-enabled XL-MIMO systems. First, we derive the effective beamfocusing distances for the long and short axes of the array. Interestingly, the radiation space of a non-square UPA can be partitioned into three regions, i.e., the fully near-field, the anisotropic near-field, and the far-field regions, and the anisotropic region asymptotically dominates the overall near-field space as the array aspect ratio increases. Then, the asymptotic effective degree of freedom for non-square UPA-enabled XL-MIMO systems is provided, which reveals that distance-domain multiplexing is governed by the long-axis aperture in the large array aspect ratio regime. Furthermore, the closed-form Cramer-Rao bound for distance estimation and the three-dimensional (3D) position error bound (PEB) are derived to reveal the geometry-induced performance trade-offs among distance, azimuth, and elevation estimation, based on which the optimal array aspect ratio that minimizes the 3D PEB is determined. Finally, by exploiting the anisotropic wavefront properties, we design a 3D anisotropic near-field codebook to facilitate low-complexity channel estimation for non-square UPAs. Numerical results validate that the proposed codebook achieves comparable accuracy to the 3D polar-domain codebook at reduced complexity.
Signal Processing.comment: 15 pages, 11 figures, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Communications

Signal Processing.title: Decision Fusion in Wireless Networks: A Tutorial and Survey of Classical and Learning-Based Methods
Signal Processing.summary: Decision fusion combines local decisions from distributed sensors to support reliable detection of phenomena in wireless networks. The effectiveness of decision fusion depends on sensing accuracy, reporting-channel reliability, and available communications and computation resources. This article surveys decision-fusion techniques for wireless sensor networks and emerging communication systems, bringing together their theoretical foundations and practical implementation requirements. We review network architectures and hard, soft, and quantized reporting strategies, and examine statistical, learning-based, game-theoretic, and heuristic fusion approaches. Advanced fusion techniques, including relay-aware combining, link-adaptive regeneration, branch selection, and likelihood approximations, are discussed with emphasis on their assumptions, information requirements, and limitations. The survey examines tradeoffs among detection performance, computational complexity, communications overhead, energy consumption, and latency. The tradeoffs are considered across representative sensing applications and emerging technologies, including massive machine-type communication, ultra-reliable low-latency communication, uncrewed aerial vehicle-assisted networks, and the massive Internet of Things. The reviewed literature highlights the importance of jointly considering sensing quality, reporting reliability, and fusion processing when selecting a suitable strategy. Finally, we identify research directions in resource-aware optimization, uncertainty calibration, and robust learning-based fusion under heterogeneous data, missing reports, and changing wireless conditions. Particular attention is given to convergence, generalization, and the costs of training and inference.
Signal Processing.comment: 36 pages, 6 figures, journal

Signal Processing.title: Industrial Viewpoints on RAN Technologies for 6G
Signal Processing.summary: Sixth-generation (6G) mobile systems have entered the standardization phase, with commercial deployments anticipated around 2030. This article presents an industrial perspective on the performance targets and key technologies shaping the 6G radio access network (RAN). It examines advances in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO), artificial intelligence (AI), waveforms, channel coding, signal constellations, integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), and the integration of terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks (NTNs). Although detailed specification work is still ahead, the scope of the 6G studies has been defined and substantial technical progress has been made. We assess the emerging technologies and design choices from the perspectives of implementation complexity, computational and energy efficiency, interoperability, deployment feasibility, and migration from 5G. By connecting research advances with practical standardization and commercialization considerations, this article aims to inform researchers and industry practitioners developing the 6G RAN.
Signal Processing.comment: to appear in the Proceedings of the IEEE

Signal Processing.title: Chirp-Permuted AFDM: A Versatile and Multifunctional Waveform for 6G
Signal Processing.summary: We present a novel multicarrier waveform, termed chirp-permuted affine frequency division multiplexing (CP-AFDM), which introduces a unique chirp-permutation domain on top of the chirp subcarriers of the conventional AFDM. Rigorous analysis of the signal model and waveform properties demonstrates that the proposed CP-AFDM waveform preserves all core characteristics of affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) - including robustness to doubly-dispersive channels, peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR), and integrated sensing and communications (ISAC)-enabling full delay-Doppler representation - while introducing a new degree-of-freedom without any loss of these properties. Given this, by exploiting the vast chirp-permutation domain, two selected exemplary multifunctional applications are presented: an index modulation (IM) technique over the permutation domain which achieves significant spectral efficiency gains, and a physical-layer security scheme that ensures practically perfect security through permutation-based keying, without requiring additional transmit energy or signaling over-head. In all, these characteristics establish CP-AFDM as a highly attractive candidate for emerging sixth generation (6G) use cases demanding reliability, sensing-awareness, and multifunctionality.

Signal Processing.title: Energy- and Thermal-Aware Resource Management on Mobile IoT Endpoints: A Survey
Signal Processing.summary: Energy-aware and thermal-aware management of computing resources on portable and mobile Internet-of-Things (IoT) endpoints is still practiced pillar by pillar: radios, processors, and flash are optimized in isolation, yet sealed system-on-chip (SoC) products share sleep states, interconnects, and thermal limits. Pillar-local joule or temperature gains therefore often disappear after integration, and published savings are frequently incomparable. This survey asks how radio, compute, and storage should be coordinated so that deep sleep remains reachable, and which reporting rules make endpoint energy and thermal claims comparable. We synthesize literature from roughly 2000 to early 2026 with three instruments: a five-phase wireless power anatomy for power-aware networking; a four-branch taxonomy for collective power--performance optimization under mixed regimes; and eight evaluation gates that separate energy outcome, control cost, thermal feasibility, and evidence quality. We qualify the radio-limited premise with compute-, storage-, and thermal-dominated counterexamples, compare modeling and monitoring families, treat thermal behaviour as a shared constraint by separating sensing interfaces, compact models, throttling actuators, and the short-peak versus sustained-throttling regimes that reverse room-temperature rankings, give an illustrative phase-budget example with a sensitivity check and a model-selection workflow, and close with open problems on composability and reproducible measurement. The intended readers work on sustainable computing, mobile systems, and embedded energy management.
Signal Processing.comment: 43 pages, 8 figures, 27 tables

Signal Processing.title: Asynchronous Uplink Rate Splitting Multiple Access
Signal Processing.summary: We study a two-user uplink system in which each user splits its message into layers and transmits them with deliberately chosen timing offsets, a scheme we call asynchronous rate splitting (A-RS). We show that timing offsets make the layers distinguishable only in the excess band of the pulse, where two spectral aliases overlap. For a root-raised-cosine pulse, the rate for every subset of layers has a scalar closed form that depends on the offsets through a single timing dispersion term. For fixed layer spectra and timing offsets, the achievable two-user rate region is a pentagon. Its two maximum-sum-rate corners are attained by successive interference cancellation that combines all matched-filter outputs at each decoding stage. Two layers per user, separated by half a symbol, are optimal for any delay between the users, and the spectrum of the user decoded last is a water-filling nested inside the water-filling of the total power. At high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the optimal spectrum has twice the density in the excess band. By using the excess bandwidth of the pulse, which synchronous transmission leaves unused, A-RS achieves rate pairs outside the regions of both synchronous and asynchronous non-orthogonal multiple access. We implement a practical system with low-density parity-check codes which gives the weaker user $0.97$ bits per symbol more than any single-stream scheme at the same SNR.

Signal Processing.title: Spectral-Leakage-Guided Phase-Noise Compensation for Sub-THz OFDM
Signal Processing.summary: Oscillator phase noise is a key impairment in sub-THz OFDM, where it spreads energy across subcarriers and generates inter-carrier interference (ICI). Since the resulting leakage depends on both the oscillator phase noise spectrum and OFDM numerology, the useful compensation dimension varies with the operating configuration. This letter develops a leakage-guided receiver framework that relates these characteristics to the retained dimension of dominant-component Least Squares (LS) compensation and its clustered-pilot support. At 130 GHz with 64-QAM, the minimum tested order achieving BER <= 10^-6 decreases from 9 at 240 kHz to 3 at 960-1920 kHz for Hexa-X Model 2, while the first 3GPP crossing at 1920 kHz occurs with Np = 13 at 38 dB. Order adaptation reduces Stage-2 arithmetic by 66%, while four-cluster pilots improve 32-dB goodput by 35% over comb allocation.

Signal Processing.title: A Generalized Framework for Structured Low-Rank Approximation and Completion
Signal Processing.summary: We formulate a generalized version of SLRA, consisting of general affine constraints, which subsumes the problems of structured low-rank matrix approximation and completion as special cases. We characterize its critical points and propose an algorithm to approximately solve the general problem. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm for stock-price forecasting, computing approximate gcd of polynomials with noisy coefficients, and time-series denoising.
Signal Processing.comment: 19 pages, 10 figures

Logic in Computer Science.title: Ensemble Logic
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Ensemble Logic (EL) is a family of modal logics whose modal parameters are terms with quantified variables. We interpret formulas over metric monoids, that is, commutative monoids equipped with translation-invariant metrics. Displacement evaluates a formula at a translated point, while bounded existence and bounded universality evaluate it at some or every point of a window of prescribed length. Quantification over points and lengths allows the same variable to occur in the parameters of several operators. This provides a common framework for temporal and spatial reasoning in discrete, dense and multi-dimensional settings. Our main result establishes a sharp undecidability boundary for satisfiability over the natural numbers: satisfiability is undecidable already for formulas $\exists N\,\exists n\,Ψ$ in which $Ψ$ is built from the letters of a fixed alphabet by conjunction, disjunction, displacement and bounded universality. We prove this by a reduction from Post's Correspondence Problem. We also present results, in part from companion work, that place this theorem in the general theory of EL. These include an atomic-displacement normal form for covariant windows and composition laws for discrete and dense time. The discrete logic admits an embedding of linear temporal logic, defines the accepting runs of every Büchi automaton, and has a sound equational calculus. For the rational logic, we show that every fixed formula can be evaluated in polynomial time on interval models in which atomic propositions are interpreted by finite unions of intervals. Finally, we represent timed words over positions and real time and compare two window geometries; with rectangular windows, two shared lengths yield undecidability on finite timed words.

Logic in Computer Science.title: What Can Postselection on Halting Decide?
Logic in Computer Science.summary: A probabilistic program can produce an answer on some runs and continue forever on others. Suppose it halts with positive probability on every input and we count only the runs that halt. Aaronson et al. showed that if the correct answer must be more than twice as likely as the wrong one, such programs decide exactly the problems solvable with a finite list of halting questions chosen in advance. They asked what happens when the correct answer need only be more likely than the wrong one. We prove that the resulting class is exactly $\boldsymbol{Δ^0_2}$: the halting questions can now be asked one at a time, with each answer helping to determine the next question. This remains true if the program must halt with probability at least 99%, or with any other prescribed rational lower bound below one. Our main technical result is the exact query bound when the program gives two guarantees. Suppose it halts with probability at least $ρ$ and, among the runs that halt, the correct answer has probability at least $a$. For rational $0 < ρ< 1$ and $1/2 < a < 1$, these programs decide exactly the problems solvable with at most $n$ halting questions chosen in advance, where $n$ is the largest integer satisfying $ρ(a/(1-a))^n \le 1$. Every value of $n$ occurs, and different values give different classes. The proof measures how much additional halting probability a change of answer requires, and counts these changes as in Ershov's hierarchy. The results extend to quantum machines with computable gates.

Logic in Computer Science.title: VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
Logic in Computer Science.summary: LLM-based formal provers often collapse the verifier's output into a pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that feeds what Lean reports (error messages with their position, verified partial proofs, and remaining goals) back into proof search. Phase 1 samples N whole proofs; Phase 2 searches a tree of verified partial proofs with a Tactician, automated step repair, a Critic that ranks states and allocates the budget, and a Retriever. On miniF2F test, VERITAS solves 86.9% with Claude Haiku 5.5 and 82.8% with GPT-6 Luna, against 71.7% and 61.1% for Best-of-5 sampling, and solves more theorems than three re-implemented feedback baselines at a third to a half of their search cost. We also evaluate on 55 combinatorics problems of CombiBench and release code and run logs at https://github.com/CoderDoge1108/VERITAS.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Coalgebraic Path Constraints
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Axiomatizing covarieties of coalgebras for an endofunctor is less intuitive than axiomatizing varieties of algebras via equations (Dahlqvist and Schmid, 2022). Existing techniques come from coalgebraic modal logic, pattern avoidance specifications, and hidden algebra. We introduce equational path constraints, a well-behaved and relatively easy to describe class of finitary behavioural properties that provide an algebra-flavoured alternative to coequations. The basic idea is to assign a pair of values to each path through a coalgebra and posit that the two values coincide. We show that equational path constraints define covarieties and construct final coalgebras relative to equational path constraints in some concrete cases. We connect equational path constraints to coequations when values computed from paths live in a monad, and we compute an upper bound on the number of colours needed to express the coequation. One of our constructions is reminiscent of the initial/terminal sequences of (Adámek, 1974) and (Barr, 1993). Motivating examples include commutativity conditions in automata theory, differential equations, bi-infinite streams, and frame conditions.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Theorems 3.26 and 4.3 are new. Discussion of frame conditions has been fleshed out. The diagram in Fig. 1 has been added to illustrate the terminal net construction. Bounded branching has been given a fuller treatment. Proofs now appear in the text

Logic in Computer Science.title: Symmetries of Dependency Quantified Boolean Formulas
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Symmetry breaking is a standard technique for reducing redundancy in automated reasoning, with well-developed theories for SAT and QBF. In this paper we study symmetries of dependency quantified Boolean formulas (DQBF), a generalisation of QBF which allows for explicit quantifier dependencies. The possibility of incomparable dependency sets makes extending existing QBF techniques non-trivial. We develop a theoretical framework for syntactic and semantic symmetries of DQBF that accounts for these dependency constraints. Building on this framework we establish a general lex-leader symmetry-breaking construction that strictly generalises the corresponding construction for QBF, using a lex-permissibility condition to ensure that local transformations respect the dependencies. We complement this construction with a canonisation method that exploits problem-specific symmetries without requiring lex-permissibility. Proof-of-concept experiments demonstrate the benefits of lex-leader symmetry breaking and the substantial additional gains provided by canonisation predicates for the succinct pigeonhole principle, although the impact of symmetry breaking is solver-dependent.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 34 pages + 5 additional pages appendix; v3 is a substantial rewriting and extension of v2

Logic in Computer Science.title: SaltBench: A Referee-Gated Protocol for Measuring Method Effects in Machine-Checked Software Work
Logic in Computer Science.summary: SaltBench asks how a machine referee changes how a coding agent works. Outcomes are decided outside the agent's toolchain; on the Claude lane a wall probed before any scored run isolates the agent from the network, reference solutions and harness, and 5 Gemini-lane cells served web search results are declared and leave every comparison; a dated freeze of predictions authorizes each run; a budget stop is a halt, never a failure. Five Rust systems components on a pinned Verus toolchain are each refereed by a withheld test suite. The arms: plain; salt-diet, also instructed to specify and verify its code (a registered reduced rendering of the method); and two arms handed the specification a priori, where the registered sign test at k=4 reached no verdict (3 of 4, p = 0.3125). salt-diet cost more on all five components, by a practical margin: no premium exceeded 2.8879x under either reading of the declared set and the three cheapest sat below 1.4x, a bound of this population and not a promise about larger ones: the premium is near 1 on the smallest components and rises with size. Versions 2 and 3 add the complete pilot matrix: 200 conditions over four models, 181 with a result of record, 16 inexpressible and 3 declared unreached at the cost cap, with no verdict on the arms. Version 3 adds a correctness reading, declared post hoc and registered after every verdict it reads existed and many had been read by its author: 447 cells pass the withheld suite, 40 fail, 10 are censored at a registered budget, 4 are unscorable and 42 are read by condition. salt-diet's pass-rate interval lies wholly below plain's on 8 greenfield and 5 brownfield rows and wholly above it on 2 greenfield rows. It is descriptive, over three cells of record per condition, with no test, and says nothing about whether the method makes code more or less correct. The full record is public.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: v5: corrects the abstract's network-isolation clause, which held for the Claude lane only; adds two temp-directory limits; adds three dated sections: a second model run on the same matrix beside a same-day control, and two first-stage reads of an explanation arm. No table of record changes. 56 pages

Logic in Computer Science.title: How many mistakes does it take to learn an interval? Exact Littlestone dimensions of intervals and their unions
Logic in Computer Science.summary: The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points, only its order of growth was known. We determine it exactly. For every switch budget $k$ (with both end labels fixed when $k$ is odd), the smallest size on which $d$ mistakes can be forced follows a three-regime law: $d+1$ while $d\le k$, then $2d-k+1$, and beyond $d=\lceil 3k/2\rceil+k-1$ doubling the size adds exactly $k$ mistakes. Unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points correspond to $k=2j$ and size $m+1$, and a single interval gives the thresholds $1,2,3,5,7,10,14,20,\dots$. The natural learner that waits for a positive example and binary-searches both endpoints is not optimal: it can be forced into one extra mistake for 50,847 of the domain sizes below $10^5$. Upper bounds come from a gap potential and a block-pairing learner, and lower bounds from adversary strategies and a refinement step. These tools give an explicit optimal learner with $O(\log m)$ time per round, which on random streams makes more mistakes on average than the natural learner. For randomised learners, we compute the randomised Littlestone dimension of thresholds exactly and prove that a greedy adversary forces an explicit closed-form number of expected mistakes on intervals; this bound is within $0.64$ of optimal and, we conjecture, exact (confirmed for $m\le70$). Exact computation tests every result, and the formulas for every switch budget are machine-checked in Lean 4.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 33 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables. Code and Lean 4 proofs: https://github.com/researchbackup27-sudo/exact-littlestone-intervals

Logic in Computer Science.title: Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers
Logic in Computer Science.summary: AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Logic in Computer Science.title: Rate--burst safety languages: the Farey structure of the burst boundary and discrimination under erasures
Logic in Computer Science.summary: A leaky-bucket constraint with rate \(ρ\) and burst \(B\) allows at most \(ρn+B\) costly steps in every window of \(n\) consecutive steps. The infinite 0/1 words that satisfy it form a safety language. For a finite graph with edge costs 0 and 1, we study the least burst at which the cost word of some infinite path lies in this language, as a function of the real rate. This function is the exact tolerance of a monitor that distinguishes two finite-state systems observed through an erasure channel with a leaky-bucket bound. The language is \(ω\)-regular at every rational rate but not at irrational rates once the burst reaches 1, so ultimately periodic witnesses do not come from automata theory. We prove directly that simple lassos suffice at all real rates and that all breakpoints of the boundary lie in the Farey sequence of order N for a graph with N vertices. One lasso has a tight bound of order N to the power 2/3 on its affine pieces, whereas the choice among paths creates downward jumps and boundaries that are neither convex nor concave. One evaluation at the mediant of each Farey interval recovers the affine piece and an optimal lasso, and a greatest-fixed-point computation over decreasing integer bursts yields the whole function in polynomial time and linear working space. We also compute discrimination horizons and extend the Farey structure to turn-based safety games.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Taint Analysis via Heap-Aware Propagation
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Taint analysis for C depends on how precisely the analysis tracks tainted values as they flow through memory objects. Without field sensitivity, a tainted object field can spuriously taint an entire object, producing significant false alarms. In this paper, we present a field-sensitive taint analysis that combines Data Structure Analysis (DSA) for field-sensitive points-to information with a data-flow analysis for tracking explicit dependencies. We identify that existing DSA-style analyses lose precision on a common object pattern: a C struct object that mixes scalar fields with a flexible array member. When such an array is accessed with symbolic indices, DSA loses points-to field sensitivity for the entire object, inflating false alarms in the data-flow analysis.
  To address this, we propose I-DSA, which extends DSA by representing field positions as intervals, so that a pointer with symbolic bounds merges only the fields within those bounds. We further develop a sound data-flow analysis based on abstract interpretation. We implement I-DSA on top of SeaDSA and the data-flow analysis inside Crab. Our tool targets LLVM IR and supports configurable taint policies by instrumenting the IR with taint intrinsics. Our experiments show that I-DSA reduces the false alarms caused by this pattern at little cost in the pointer analysis, that SVF, an inclusion-based pointer analysis, shows a similar field-sensitivity loss, and that our taint analysis scales better than PhASAR on real-world programs.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: This is an extended version of the VMCAI 2027 paper. The artifact is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19826762

Logic in Computer Science.title: Bound to be Complete: Efficient Verification for SQL Equivalence via U-Expressions
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Automated verification of SQL query equivalence is a fundamental problem in database area. Recent works developed verifiers with guaranteed completeness, which can generate counterexamples to disprove non-equivalent queries and are useful in various scenarios. However, they have to solve complex formulas and can fail to produce counterexamples within a reasonable time budget.
  This paper presents a new complete verifier called SQLution, which not only greatly reduces the verification time, but also supports more SQL features. The key insight is to represent SQL semantics using U-expression, a functional algebra that can model SQL with significantly simpler formulas than prior works, thereby leading to more efficient SMT solving. To turn this insight into a practical verifier, SQLution further tackles two technical challenges associated with modeling SQL using U-expression, namely, the lack of tuple ordering and the presence of unbounded summations. In particular, to support tuple ordering, SQLution proposes order semantics encoding which combines U-expressions with first-order logic. To handle unbounded summation, SQLution introduces unbounded summation expansion to transform them into bounded summations, which can be directly encoded into FOL formulas. Evaluation shows that compared with state-of-the-art verifiers, SQLution can support all 271 non-equivalent query pairs derived from the Spider dataset and reduces verification time by up to 98.6%.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Extending CDCL to disjunctions of parity equations
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Problems provably hard for Resolution are also provably hard for CDCL, but shorter proofs can sometimes be found using stronger proof systems such as Res($\oplus$), a generalization of Resolution to XNF formulas, whose constraints are disjunctions of parity equations, called linear clauses. While some solvers like CryptoMiniSat reason on Boolean clauses with separate parity equations in a system called CNF-XOR, general XNF reasoning is less explored.
  We present CDCL($\oplus$), a generalization of CDCL to XNF formulas that includes branching on arbitrary parity equations, linear-algebraic reasoning during unit propagation, and learning linear clauses in conflict analysis. Our key tool is the affine resolution rule, which generalizes classical resolution and allows translations of 1-UIP clause learning and variable elimination. We develop a theory of UIPs to show that we learn an asserting clause with the largest possible backjump, the same guarantee as classical CDCL. We prove that CDCL($\oplus$) not only produces Res($\oplus$) proofs, but also polynomially simulates Res($\oplus$) given nondeterministic decisions and restarts, much like the relationship between CDCL and Resolution.
  We implement CDCL($\oplus$) in our solver Xorcle, which cleanly adapts over a dozen major classical CDCL heuristics. We introduce the CSIDS decision heuristic, which selects decisions from activity-ranked clauses, and the LRUP($\oplus$) proof logging format. On a suite of cryptographic benchmarks, Xorcle is generally competitive with or outperforms Kissat, CaDiCaL, and CryptoMiniSat, and beats the concurrently developed XNF solver Xorricane. Additionally, Xorcle's reasoning and search alone (i.e., without detecting XORs) solves CNF versions of Tseitin formulas, perfect matching formulas, and bijective pigeonhole formulas with $n+1$ pigeons into $n$ holes using apparently polynomial running time.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: v2: 60 pages, 4 figures. This updated version includes a new backjump optimality theorem, more translated heuristics, and a more extensive evaluation of Xorcle. In preparation for a journal submission. v1: 28 pages, 5 figures. This is the extended version of an article to appear in SAT'26 (29th International Conference on Theory and Applications of Satisfiability Testing)

Logic in Computer Science.title: Lean Census: A Distributional Analysis of AI-Generated Lean Code
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We compare two human-written and four AI-generated Lean libraries with Mathlib through the distributions of simple statistics of their code. For each library we measure inline claims in proofs, proof length, how often each declaration is used, and design choices such as instances and private declarations, and we read each against the variation among Mathlib's own areas. The AI-generated libraries have more inline claims per theorem, longer proofs, fewer instances, and more private declarations than the human-written ones. We release the code for the analysis as a package, lean-census, at https://github.com/project-numina/lean-census.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 16 pages, 17 figures. Code at https://github.com/project-numina/lean-census

Logic in Computer Science.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Proof-assistant kernels with strict propositions---Lean 4, Agda's Prop, and Coq/Rocq's SProp---build proof irrelevance into conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$), equating all derivations of a theorem. While natural for pure mathematics, judgmental proof irrelevance breaks provenance in verified scientific stores, where predicates, refinements, and institutional maps must distinguish independent derivations for consilience and counterfactual retraction; with subsingleton elimination, it also breaks normalization and algorithmic transitivity.
  We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a kernel for provenance-preserving scientific stores. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes (Prop, Set, $\mathsf{Type}_k$ for $k \ge 1$), impredicative Prop, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types: conversion $\equiv$ is untyped orthogonal-CRS joinability, while proof irrelevance is a witnessed axiom ($\mathsf{irrel} : ΠP:\mathsf{Prop}.\,Πp,q:P.\,\mathsf{Id}\,P\,p\,q$). Second, coercion-free subsumption unifies cumulativity, $Π$-covariant subtyping, and ontology inclusions; its bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction, match declarative typing, and compile to heuristic-free checkers ($\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1$) sound and complete relative to strong normalization. Third, we link external verifiers via constructive institutions (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize justification logic with Why-provenance $\mathsf{supp}(j,P)$, and type open-world knowledge graphs via TTR. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Guard Analysis and Safe Erasure Gradual Typing: a Type System for Elixir
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
We formalize a new type system for Elixir, a dynamically typed functional programming language of growing popularity that runs on the Erlang virtual machine. Our system combines gradual typing with semantic subtyping to enable precise, sound, and practical static type analysis, without requiring any changes to Elixir's compilation pipeline or runtime. Type soundness is ensured by leveraging runtime checks -- both implicit, from the Erlang VM, and explicit, via developer-written guards.
  Central to our approach are two key innovations: the notion of "strong functions", which can be assigned precise types even when applied to inputs that may fall outside their intended domain; and a fine-grained analysis of guards that enables accurate type refinement for case expressions and guarded function definitions. While type information is erased before execution and not used by the compiler, our "safe erasure" gradual typing strategy maintains soundness and expressiveness without compromising compatibility or performance. This work lays the theoretical foundation for Elixir's new type system, outlines its integration into recent versions of the language, and demonstrates its effectiveness on large-scale industrial codebases.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Characterization and Decidability of FC-Definable Regular Languages
Logic in Computer Science.summary: FC is a first-order logic that reasons over all factors of a finite word using concatenation, and can define non-regular languages like that of all squares (ww). In this paper, we establish that there are regular languages that are not FC-definable. Moreover, we give a decidable characterization of the FC-definable regular languages in terms of algebra, automata, and regular expressions. The latter of which is natural and concise: Star-free generalized regular expressions extended with the Kleene star of terminal words.

Logic in Computer Science.title: QANAD: A Model-Driven Framework for Quantitative Analysis and Synthesis of Activity Diagrams via Probabilistic Model Checking
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Probabilistic model checking is a widely used formal verification technique to automatically verify qualitative and quantitative QoS properties for probabilistic models, such as reliability, performance, and cost. However, devising suitable and representative models for systems of interest in model checkers, writing corresponding properties, and verifying them requires domain knowledge in probabilistic models, formal verification, and the target model checkers. This unavoidably makes model checking not easily accessible for researchers and engineers who may lack the required knowledge. Previous work has extended UML activity diagrams with probability and time, along with quality annotations, developed transformations from activity diagrams to probabilistic models which model checkers support, and implemented accompanying tools for automation. The research, however, is fragmented, informal, or not fully open, making its use, extension, and adaptation non-trivial. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce QANAD, a comprehensive verification framework for activity diagrams, that includes a new profile for probability, time, parameters, and quality annotations, a semantics interpretation of activity diagrams in Markov models variants (DTMCs, MDPs, and CTMCs) and their parametric versions, and a set of formal transformation rules from activity diagrams to the PRISM modelling language, supported by the leading model checkers PRISM and Storm. The theory underpinning QANAD has been realised into transformation implementation using model-driven engineering, enabling fully automated model transformation with automated verification using (parametric) probabilistic model checking and semi-automated synthesis. We demonstrate QANAD on a case study where multiple robots are used for delivery in a hospital environment and evaluated six other examples from the literature.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Accepted version by the journal of Software and Systems Modeling (SoSyM)

Logic in Computer Science.title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 24 pages, 5 figures

Logic in Computer Science.title: Bounded Treewidth Rulesets Are Not Finitely Controllable
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
An ontology language $O$ is finitely controllable with respect to a query language $Q$ if the finite and unrestricted variants of the query entailment problem for $\langle O, Q\rangle$ coincide. In this paper, we study finite controllability (FC) in its classical sense for existential rules, where $O$ is a class of existential rules and $Q$ is the class of all Boolean conjunctive queries (BCQs).
  A natural question in this line of work is whether the class of bounded treewidth sets (BTS) is finitely controllable with respect to BCQs. We answer this question negatively: we exhibit a simple set of rules over a binary signature and prove that it is BTS but not FC. Moreover, using the same set of rules, we show that two subclasses of BTS, namely GBTS and pieceful, are not FC either.

Logic in Computer Science.title: No Perfect Guardrail & No Perfect Guard: On the Decidability of Output Policies for Large Language Models
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Expecting guardrails to provide a general guarantee of safety fails to recognize the limits of computational enforcement and policy specification. We argue that promising such perfection is an ethical failure of precision, and that invoking it to abdicate responsibility is a moral failure. Guardrails can support responsible action, but cannot relieve researchers, developers, policymakers, or users of their obligations to examine what they claim, permit, and prevent.
  We establish a precise computational boundary. If every finite string is a possible output of a language model, a computable guard that blocks every forbidden output and passes every permitted one exists if and only if the policy is decidable. For an undecidable policy, every guard misclassifies infinitely many strings, and every guard that blocks all forbidden outputs excludes infinitely many permitted ones. We apply this characterization to arithmetic truth, program behavior, and harmful instructions to an idealized recipient. We distinguish guards from execution monitors, identify bounded and interceptable cases admitting exact enforcement, and explain why the results establish no positive lower bound on average error.
  Exact enforcement does not establish that a policy adequately captures safety. Conservative exclusion may withhold warnings, remedies, or challenges needed to recognize the policy's own defects. Human oversight cannot substitute for judgment: an apparent controller can become an instrument of purposes they have ceased to examine. Responsible governance requires continued critical challenge and the intellectual and moral humility to recognize possible flaws in our machines, rules, policies, and ourselves. The impossibility of a general assurance of perfection is a condition responsible practice must confront, not a responsibility that another guardrail - or another guard - can remove.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 31 pages, including a one-page executive summary and a self-contained proof appendix. Sustainable Systems Laboratory Technical Report SSL-TR-2026-002, Preprint v0.1

Logic in Computer Science.title: Moonshine Conjecture Formalized
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
The celebrated and intimidating Moonshine Conjecture has now been formalized in Lean. This achievement might suggest that, once a sufficiently large library compiles, the principal mathematical work is complete. This paper tells a less optimistic story.
  During our formalization project, we repeatedly encountered two problems that a formally checked proof alone does not settle: (1) whether the formal statements actually express the mathematics we humans expect, and (2) how that meaning survives as the repositories and their dependencies evolve.
  We argue that there is no magic pill that turns a large agent-produced library into mathematics a community can trust. Even after the proofs are checked by the Lean kernel, someone must judge whether the definitions and statements express the intended mathematics and whether future updates preserve that meaning. This work, even when done, can only be trusted. We must therefore return to the usual trust model: relying on the mathematical judgment of maintainers and expert communities.
  But semantic review is expensive, making it tempting to keep producing code and take successful kernel checks as sufficient grounds for trust. This shortcut accumulates semantic debt: definitions and results with unchecked mathematical interpretations are reused as foundations for further work. A library may keep compiling and produce the desired formal theorem while users lose track of which mathematical claims they can responsibly rely on.
  Reliable reuse is also a prerequisite for Terence Tao's vision of formal mathematics as something people can navigate, explain, learn from, and build with. This paper takes our work connecting the VOA and CFSG repositories for the Moonshine Conjecture as a case study of the challenges of reliable reuse as formal developments scale.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 7 pages, 0 figures. A case study in Lean formalization, semantic trust, and repository versioning

Logic in Computer Science.title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available.
  The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals.
  We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 16 pages, 9 tables, 1 figure

Logic in Computer Science.title: Compiling Existential-Positive Queries to Bounded-Variable Fragments
Logic in Computer Science.summary: A crucial property of bounded-variable fragments of first-order logic is that they can be evaluated in polynomial time. It is therefore a useful preprocessing step to rewrite, if possible, a first-order query to a logically equivalent one with a minimum number of variables. However, it may occur that reducing the number of variables causes an increase in formula size. We investigate this trade-off for the existential-positive fragment of first-order queries, where variable minimisation is decidable in general. In particular, we study the blow-up in the formula size when compiling existential-positive queries to the bounded variable fragment of positive first-order logic. While the increase of the formula size is always at most exponential, we identify situations (based on the signature and the number of variables) where only a polynomial blow-up is needed. In all other cases, we show that an exponential lower bound on the formula size of the compiled formula that matches the general upper bound. This exponential lower bound is unconditional, and is the first unconditional lower bound for formula size with respect to the studied compilation; it is proved via establishing a novel interface with circuit complexity which may be of future interest.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Version of an article that appeared in PODS '19

Logic in Computer Science.title: When are two algorithms the same? Towards addressing Hilbert's 24th problem
Logic in Computer Science.summary: The informal question of when two theorem proofs are "essentially the same" goes back to David Hilbert, who considered adding it (or something largely equivalent) to his famous list of open problems, but eventually decided to leave it out. Given that the notion of a formal proof is closely related to that of a (computer) program, i.e. a recursive function, it may be useful to ask the same question with regard to programs instead. Here we propose a minimalistic approach to this question within Recursion Theory, building heavily on the use of Kolmogorov Complexity.

Logic in Computer Science.title: The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts.
  The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 9 pages

Logic in Computer Science.title: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained control over key properties such as constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and data generation and alignment strategies. In particular, it allows the use of rich constraints over infinite domains, and uses solvers to ensure that the constraints are meaningful and that generated samples satisfy the constraints.
  We design NeSySy to support both learning with declarative constraints and learning from distant supervision. Across a range of constraint families, we provide evidence that its parameters induce systematic and largely independent effects on task difficulty. Using NeSySy, we study constraint-aware learning methods, identifying regimes where explicit constraint enforcement is beneficial and where expressive unconstrained models can instead learn constraint structure directly from data. Our results establish NeSySy as a controlled testbed for analysing the interaction between learning and logical structure.
  NeSySy is built around a pipeline that incorporates solvers. Satisfiability checkers (CNFgen and Z3) generate and certify constraints. Constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) compute optimal repairs that guarantee every generated sample is consistent.

Logic in Computer Science.title: On the semantics of conditional branching
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Motivated by the non-standard interpretations of if-then-else in probabilistic and quantum programs we review the different semantics of conditional branching and propose a unifying categorical structure for the interpretation of if-then-else. We show that many semantically important categories possess this structure, covering inter alia classical, probabilistic, quantum or non-deterministic computations. We examine algebraic structures related to and generated by this categorical structure, in particular on collections of predicates. In this setting we show that the skew-associativity rules of GKATs and barycentric algebras are two instances of a common skew-associativity rule.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 31 pages, proofs in the Appendix

Logic in Computer Science.title: Inductive Grounded Arithmetic: Goodstein, the Hydra, and $Γ_0$
Logic in Computer Science.summary: What does a recursive definition mean in a grounded logic, where a sentence is true only if a terminating process makes it so? This paper takes Kripke's answer for truth, the least fixed point, as a rule. Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) writes any recursive definition as one self-referential term; Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA) adds the elimination rule for every positive one, making each an inductive definition. IGA is omega-sound and proof-grounded: sound and complete for a semantics whose certificates are its own proofs. IGA proves Goodstein's theorem, the Kirby-Paris hydra game for primitive recursive strategies, and, along Gentzen's route, the consistency of Peano Arithmetic. IGA certifies the Veblen notation below every $\varphi(n,0)$: its accessibility ordinal there is $\varphi(ω,0)$, that of the paracomplete truth theory PKF. Every theorem is machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL; order types and PKF's ordinal are cited. IGA proves the Veblen notation well-founded exactly when it admits bivalence of accessibility for it, which it does not, and that bivalence is sound exactly when the order is well-founded. So $Γ_0$ lies exactly one instance of excluded middle away, and that instance, the well-foundedness sentence and one membership claim in an internal form of Kleene's $\mathcal{O}$ are interderivable over IGA. Bivalence at the Bachmann-Howard order keeps proof-groundedness. One such claim buys well-foundedness of the countable part of Buchholz's notation at every finite level, of type $ψ_0(Ω_ω)$, and $k$ stratified bivalence rules give a proof-grounded system proving the countable part up to level $k$ well-founded; $k$ iterated closings-off of truth do too, sound only for a closed-off model. Unrestricted conditional proof is inconsistent (Curry's paradox); the purchase is implication at a hypothesis not provably decided.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: major revision, now 79 pages

Logic in Computer Science.title: Similarity-based OSF Logic for Flexible SPARQL Query Answering
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We present an updated version of fosf, a reasoner for fuzzy order-sorted feature (OSF) logic, with support for flexible SPARQL query answering over RDF knowledge graphs. Fuzzy OSF logic is a knowledge representation and reasoning language where feature symbols denote functions and sort symbols denote fuzzy sets. Sorts are organized in a fuzzy subsumption relation that extends to OSF terms, record-like structures representing classes of entities. The unification algorithm for these structures provides a calculus of fuzzy type subsumption. The latest release of fosf introduces support for similarity-based reasoning by extending the OSF language with a similarity relation among sorts, alongside a translation engine for compiling OSF terms into standard SPARQL. Queries expressed as OSF terms undergo fuzzy ontology-aware rewriting prior to translation. This process incorporates an OSF theory of sort definitions, feature domain and range declarations, and fuzzy subsumption and similarity relations through fuzzy OSF constraint normalization. This rewriting enables flexible query answering by returning approximate solutions, allowing queries that would otherwise be inconsistent with the underlying ontology to yield relevant results.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Accepted at ISWC 2026 (Demo)

Logic in Computer Science.title: Invariance and Expressiveness: Modal Variations
Logic in Computer Science.summary: This contribution focuses on bisimulation invariance as the hallmark of modal model theory and of modal modelling. It exemplifies traditional as well as more recent ramifications \&\ extensions of classical results -- involving variant modes of bisimulation equivalence and matching modalities also beyond plain Kripke structures, and emphasising especially the technical challenges in finite model theory and other non-elementary settings. Main results to be discussed revolve about the theme of expressive completeness phenomena: beside expressive completeness under bisimulation invariance in relation to first-order background logics, in the style of van Benthem--Rosen characterisations, this also concerns maximality results under criteria form abstract model theory, in the style of Lindstroem theorems.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: this is a draft for a chapter in a forthcoming handbook on Comtemporary Modal Logic

Logic in Computer Science.title: Oddomorphisms, Split-Off Minors, and the Strong Roberson Conjecture
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We show that the existence of an oddomorphism from a graph $F$ to a graph $G$ does not imply that $G$ is a minor of $F$. This answers a question posed by Roberson (2026) and shows that the CFI graphs cannot be used to prove the Strong Roberson Conjecture. Additionally, we introduce the concept of a split-off minor and show that the existence of an oddomorphism from $F$ to $G$ implies that $G$ is a split-off minor of $F$. Consequently, every class that is closed under taking split-off minors and disjoint unions is homomorphism distinguishing closed. The split-off minor relation is the first minor-like structural relation shown to have this property, marking a meaningful advancement in our understanding of the interaction between structural graph containment and homomorphism indistinguishability relations.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: To appear in the proceedings of CSL 2027. 22 pages. Simplified proof of Theorem 6, improved exposition, and updated references

Logic in Computer Science.title: A type theory for invertibility in weak $ω$-categories
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We present a conservative extension ICaTT of the dependent type theory Catt for weak $ω$-categories with a type witnessing coinductive invertibility of cells. This extension allows for a concise description of the ``walking equivalence'' as a context, and of a set of maps characterising $ω$-equifibrations as substitutions. We provide an implementation of our theory, which we use to formalise basic properties of invertible cells. These properties allow us to give semantics of ICaTT in marked weak $ω$-categories, building a fibrant marked $ω$-category out of every model of ICaTT.

Logic in Computer Science.title: The Necessity of Acceptance & Rejection in Inferential Reasoning
Logic in Computer Science.summary: In this paper, we argue that acceptance and rejection constitute two fundamental positions necessary for inferential reasoning. Our central thesis is that a proposition acquires an inferential role when it is considered from a position of acceptance or rejection, rather than purely understood as propositional content. We distinguish between understanding a proposition, entertaining it hypothetically, and employing it within an inference. Particular attention is given to hypothetical reasoning and suspended judgement, which appear to challenge the necessity of adopting either position. We maintain that these cases do not undermine our thesis, since inferential reasoning can involve provisional acceptance or rejection without requiring personal belief or permanent commitment. Accordingly, the necessity of these positions should be understood as inferential rather than psychological. By examining the relationship between propositional content, inferential positions, and rational commitment, we defend the view that acceptance and rejection provide the fundamental conditions under which propositions can function within reasoning. This establishes a philosophical foundation for understanding inference through opposed rational positions.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 11 Pages

Logic in Computer Science.title: Revisiting Finiteness of Matrix Monoids
Logic in Computer Science.summary: This paper concerns decision problems related to finite monoids of rational matrices. We show that determining finiteness of a given finitely presented monoid is in PSPACE, improving the known $\text{co}{-}\text{NEXP}^{\text{NP}}$ bound. We also show that the membership problem for finite matrix monoids is PSPACE-complete, improving the known NEXP-upper bound. Our two complexity results are corollaries of a new polynomial bit-size bound on matrix entries in finite monoids. This is obtained by reduction to the case of matrix groups, using the structure theory of noncommutative algebras and of matrix monoids. Our techniques also give us a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding whether a monoid of rational matrices is conjugate to a monoid of integer matrices.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 17 pages, published at ICALP 2026

Logic in Computer Science.title: Burnside Problems for Matrix Semigroup Quotients with Applications to Border Complexity
Logic in Computer Science.summary: The Burnside theorem for matrix semigroups states that a finitely generated matrix semigroup is finite whenever each element has only finitely many distinct powers. We study analogous finiteness questions for quotients of matrix semigroups by congruences, which need not themselves admit faithful finite-dimensional matrix representations. We show three finiteness criteria based on uniform bounds on the quotient images of (rank-)stable subsemigroups and groups in the Zariski closure. Our proofs use exterior algebra and the Ramsey theorem to develop variations of Simon's factorisation forest to matrix semigroups modulo congruences. We also present applications of our results to border complexity. One such involves separating homogeneous algebraic branching programs of fixed width and degree from its Zariski closure.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 51 pages, submitted to STOC 2027

Logic in Computer Science.title: Formal Verification of Continuous-Variable Quantum Programs
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Continuous-variable quantum computing (CQC) is a promising paradigm already accessible through public cloud services. Yet, unlike discrete-variable quantum computing (DQC), CQC lacks a formal program logic. Extending existing quantum Hoare logics to CQC poses fundamental challenges: continuous-variable quantum programs act on {\em infinite-dimensional} Hilbert spaces; their measurement outcomes are often {\em unbounded}, so expectation values may {\em diverge}. We overcome these challenges to give a formal semantics to a universal programming language for CQC and, to our knowledge, provide the first Hoare logic for CQC. We introduce an assertion language based on polynomials over canonical observables and establish soundness and relative completeness of the resulting logic. We also implement a symbolic weakest-precondition calculator for CQC. Our tool has successfully verified CQC algorithms from textbooks and calculated their approximation errors for physically realizable implementations, proved the correctness (i.e., equivalence) of gate decompositions for CQC hardware, and computed the resource requirements (i.e., number of photon-number states) for achieving a desired accuracy in the classical simulation of continuous-variable quantum programs.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Variational Trajectory Flow Matching with a Non-Linear Interpolant
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Simulation-free methods such as Trajectory Flow Matching learn dynamics by regressing the time derivative of a local interpolant placed between consecutive observations. The interpolant defines the regression target, and under sparse, irregular sampling, it underrepresents the dynamics and bounds what can be learned. We show that no fixed interpolant dominates: the best of linear, quadratic, spline and quintic changes with the system and with the sampling density. We propose to learn the interpolant instead. An amortized implicit neural representation (INR) is fitted to the training trajectories and frozen as a teacher supplying the target velocity to a learnable velocity field. We further frame the velocity field within a variational framework, yielding a probabilistic forecaster that, at inference, requires only the velocity field and no SDE solver. We evaluate our method on a range of dynamical systems: it consistently achieves high accuracy and more stable long-horizon rollouts under sparser observations, at matched velocity-field capacity.

Logic in Computer Science.title: From Innermost to Full Almost-Sure Termination of Probabilistic Term Rewriting
Logic in Computer Science.summary: There are many evaluation strategies for term rewrite systems, but proving termination automatically is usually easiest for innermost rewriting. Several syntactic criteria exist when innermost termination implies full termination. We adapt these criteria to the probabilistic setting, e.g., we show when it suffices to analyze almost-sure termination (AST) w.r.t. innermost rewriting to prove full AST of probabilistic term rewrite systems (PTRSs). These criteria also apply to other notions of termination like positive AST. We implemented and evaluated our new contributions in the tool AProVE.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Proving Almost-Sure Innermost Termination of Probabilistic Term Rewriting Using Dependency Pairs
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Dependency pairs are one of the most powerful techniques to analyze termination of term rewrite systems (TRSs) automatically. We adapt the dependency pair framework to the probabilistic setting in order to prove almost-sure innermost termination of probabilistic TRSs. To evaluate its power, we implemented the new framework in our tool AProVE.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Full version of a paper which appeared in the Proceedings of CADE 2023

Logic in Computer Science.title: Computational trust as intuitionistic knowledge
Logic in Computer Science.summary: In this paper, we will argue that the notion of computational trust can be understood as a form of fallible intuitionistic knowledge grounded in verification. This approach naturally captures a key aspect of trust: it involves vulnerability. Specifically, it validates the principle that verification leads to trust but does not validate the opposite principle that trust leads to verification. Thus, we can trust on good grounds that some program will perform according to its specification but the program might still fail. We present a simple logic for capturing this notion of computational trust based on constructive modal propositional logic extended with a trust modality, which will be specified in an inferential fashion and by utilizing the proofs-as-programs correspondence.

Logic in Computer Science.title: DARSY: A Tool for Data-Driven Abstraction and Policy Synthesis for Stochastic Systems with Unknown Dynamics
Logic in Computer Science.summary: This paper presents DARSY: a software tool for abstraction-based verification and policy synthesis in discrete-time stochastic control systems with unknown dynamics and noise distributions. DARSY requires only a simulator of the system and a Lipschitz bound on its dynamics, and needs no knowledge of dynamics or noise distributions. The tool is fully automated and constructs a finite interval Markov decision process (IMDP) abstraction from sampled transitions, whose probability intervals are obtained via statistical techniques and Lipschitz reasoning. Robust dynamic programming on this IMDP then yields a policy together with a lower bound on the probability that the unknown system satisfies a desired specification. This lower bound holds with a user-specified confidence; that is, it is probably approximately correct (PAC). The tool is implemented in Python and supports general Lipschitz-continuous system dynamics and specifications expressed in syntactically co-safe LTL (scLTL), which includes reach-avoid and finite-horizon safety specifications as special cases. Beyond standard IMDPs, DARSY implements a two-layer IMDP (2IMDP) abstraction that also bounds the probability of transitioning to aggregated state blocks, yielding smaller abstraction errors than IMDP abstractions and, as a result, tighter satisfaction guarantees. We demonstrate DARSY's broad applicability across a variety of benchmarks and specifications.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: The tool DARSY and all benchmarks are available at https://github.com/tbadings/darsy

Logic in Computer Science.title: On the Informativeness of Structural Stability Bounds for GNNs: GINs versus GATs
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Stability bounds for graph neural networks limit how much node representations can drift when the graph changes, but they are rarely compared with the simplest alternative: a bound on the distance between any two outputs, whatever the graph. We derive structural stability bounds for Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) and single-head GATv1 networks under deterministic edge perturbations that need not be small, and compare each with such a perturbation-independent diameter bound. For GINs, we characterize exactly when the stability bound is tighter, through a condition linking perturbation size, depth and maximum degree; it holds with a wide margin on Cora, but fails beyond a few layers on the low-degree MUTAG graphs. For GATv1, the bound is never tighter, which calls for analyses based on attention masses.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Extended version of a paper submitted to ESANN 2027

Logic in Computer Science.title: Compact MaxSAT Encodings for Balanced Waiting in B2B Meeting Scheduling
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Business-to-business (B2B) meeting schedules can leave participants with long and uneven waits. Earlier break-based B2B models count interruptions without measuring their duration. Our earlier work minimizes the range of participant idle totals, but a minimum range can still leave long waits. We study lexicographic optimization of idle range, maximum idle, and total idle, in that order. Waiting is measured in empty slots between a participant's first and last meetings. Balance compares idle totals among participants requesting at least two meetings. Using weighted maximum satisfiability (MaxSAT), we prove preservation of feasible schedules, objective costs, and priorities. Compact-Base retains our earlier feasibility encoding; Compact-Objective adds objective-specific representations. We compare both with Direct, an independent implementation based on the 2022 MaxSAT model. Encoding comparisons use three repetitions per encoding-objective-instance combination on 226 variants of 20 base instances. Schedule-quality comparisons use break, range, and lexicographic objectives with the same encoding and feasible set. Across nine objective-dataset comparisons, Compact-Objective had the lowest median clause count and lower median peak memory than Direct. Runtime rankings changed in comparisons with the same solver build and computing environment. On 84 instances solved optimally under all three quality objectives, selected lexicographic schedules preserved the optimal idle range. Compared with selected range-only schedules, maximum idle decreased on 11 instances and total idle on 56. On 68 instances also solved optimally under range-then-total optimization, the selected schedules matched the three-tier criterion values. Compact-Base supplied the larger clause reduction relative to Direct; Compact-Objective reduced clauses further.
